Safe Testing

Peter Grünwald Affiliation: Leiden University, Leiden, The Netherlands    Rianne de Heide Affiliation: Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam, The Netherlands Affiliation: r.de.heide@vu.nl    Wouter M. Koolen Affiliation: University of Twente, Enschede, The Netherlands Affiliation: Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, Amsterdam, The Netherlands Affiliation: {\{pdg, wmkoolen}\}@cwi.nl
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We develop the theory of hypothesis testing based on the e-value, a notion of evidence that, unlike the p-value, allows for effortlessly combining results from several studies in the common scenario where the decision to perform a new study may depend on previous outcomes. Tests based on e-values are safe, i.e. they preserve Type-I error guarantees, under such optional continuation. We define growth-rate optimality (GRO) as an analogue of power in an optional continuation context, and we show how to construct GRO e-variables for general testing problems with composite null and alternative, emphasizing models with nuisance parameters. GRO e-values take the form of Bayes factors with special priors. We illustrate the theory using several classic examples including a one-sample safe tt-test and the 2×22\times 2 contingency table. Sharing Fisherian, Neymanian and Jeffreys-Bayesian interpretations, e-values may provide a methodology acceptable to adherents of all three schools.

Keywords:

Bayes Factors, E-Values, Hypothesis Testing, Information Projection, Optional Stopping, Test Martingales

1 Introduction and Overview

We wish to test the veracity of a null hypothesis ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, often in contrast with some alternative hypothesis ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, where both ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} represent sets of distributions on some given sample space. Our theory is based on e-test statistics. These are simply nonnegative random variables that satisfy the inequality:

for all P∈ℋ0:𝐄P[E]≤1.\text{for all $P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}$:}\ \ {\bf E}_{P}[E]\leq 1. (1)

We refer to e-test statistics as e-variables, and to the value they take on a given sample as the e-value, emphasizing that they are to be viewed as an alternative to, and in many cases an improvement of, the classical p-value. Note that large e-values correspond to evidence against the null: for given e-variable EE and 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1, we define the threshold test corresponding to EE with significance level α\alpha, as the test that rejects ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} iff E≥1/αE\geq 1/\alpha. We will see, in a sense to be made more precise, that this test is safe under optional continuation with respect to Type-I error.

Motivation

p-values and standard null hypothesis testing have come under intense scrutiny in recent years (Wasserstein et al., 2016, Benjamin et al., 2018). e-variables and safe tests offer several advantages. Most importantly, in contrast to p-values, e-variables behave excellently under optional continuation, the highly common practice in which the decision to perform additional tests partly depends on the outcome of previous tests. They thus seem particularly promising when used in meta-analysis (ter Schure and Grünwald, 2019). A second reason is their enhanced interpretability: they have a very concrete (monetary) interpretation as ‘evidence against the null’ which remains valid even if one dismisses concepts such as ‘significance’ altogether, as recently advocated by Amrhein et al. (2019). A third is their flexibility: as we show in this paper, e-variables can be based on Bayesian prior knowledge, on earlier data, but also on minimax performance considerations, in all cases preserving frequentist Type I error guarantees.

Overall Contribution and Contents

Although the concept is much older (Section 7), the interest in e-values and the related test martingales has exploded over the last three years (Wang and Ramdas, 2020, Vovk and Wang, 2021, Shafer, 2021, Henzi and Ziegel, 2022, Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2021, Orabona and Jun, 2021). In this paper, we further develop the theory of e-values, by providing general optimality criteria and show how to design e-variables that satisfy them. We do this on the basis of four ever more general versions of a single novel theorem, Theorem 1. In its first incarnation, in Section 2, Theorem 1 already tells us that one can design nontrivial, useful e-variables for a wide class of testing problems with composite null and alternative. This first instance relies on using a prior W1W_{1} on the alternative ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. The ensuing e-variables, while guaranteeing frequentist Type-I error control, will have a GRO (growth-rate optimality) property under W1W_{1}. This GRO e-variable will be a Bayes factor with a special prior on the null. More general versions of the theorem allow us to construct e-variables when no prior on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is available. These satisfy either a direct worst-case optimality criterion (GROW) or a relative one (REGROW). In our example applications we restrict ourselves to classical testing scenarios such as 1-dimensional exponential families, the 2×22\times 2 contingency table, and the tt-test. Importantly, the latter two have nuisance parameters and the GRO approach provides a generic methodology for dealing with them. For the tt-test setting, GRO e-variables turn out to be Bayes factors based on the right Haar prior, as known from objective Bayes analyses (Berger et al., 1998). For the 2×22\times 2-setting, GRO e-values do not correspond to standard Bayes factors.

We then, in Section 5 and 6, investigate optional continuation, stopping and GRO in more detail, and we assess how competitive the e-variables we designed are compared to classical methods in terms of the amount of data needed before a certain desired power or growth rate can be reached. The final three sections put our work in context. We provide a historical overview of e-value related work in Section 7, critically discuss GRO in Section 8, and then, in Section 9, taking a step back, we come to the inescapable conclusion that e-variables unify and correct ideas from the three main paradigms of testing: Fisherian, Neyman-Pearsonian and Jeffreysian. But first, in the remainder of this introduction, we explain the three main interpretations of e-variables (Section 1.1), we briefly introduce our main theorem (Section 1.2) and, in Section 1.3, we explain the main advantage of e-variables over p-values in terms of optional continuation. We claim no technical novelty for this part, which mainly restates and reinterprets existing results11 1 Since the first version of the present paper appeared on arXiv, various subsets of these results have been widely discussed in various recent papers, but we still re-state them here to keep the paper self-contained. . We defer to the appendices all longer proofs and details that would distract from the main story.

1.1 The three main interpretations of e-variables

1. First Interpretation: Gambling

The first and foremost interpretation of e-variables is in terms of money, or, more precisely, Kelly (1956) gambling. Imagine a ticket (contract, gamble, investment) that one can buy for 1$, and that, after realisation of the data, pays E$E\,\$; one may buy several and positive fractional amounts of tickets. (1) says that, if the null hypothesis is true, then one expects not to gain any money by buying such tickets: for any r∈ℝ+r\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, upon buying rr tickets one expects to end up with r𝐄[E]≤r$r\mathbf{E}[E]\leq r\,\$. Therefore, if the observed value of EE is large, say 20=1/0.0520=1/0.05, one would have gained a lot of money after all, indicating that something might be wrong about the null.

2. Second Interpretation: Conservative p-Value, Type I Error Probability

Recall that a (strict) p-value is a random variable p such that for all 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1, all P0∈ℋ0P_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{0},

P0​(p≤α)=α.P_{0}(\text{\it p}\leq\alpha)=\alpha. (2)

A conservative p-value is a random variable for which (2) holds with ‘==’ replaced by ‘≤\leq’. There is a close connection between (small) p- and (large) e-values:

Proposition 1.

For any given e-variable EE, define p[e]≔1/E\text{\it p}_{[\text{\it e}]}\coloneqq 1/E. Then p[e]\text{\it p}_{[\text{\it e}]} is a conservative p-value. As a consequence, for every e-variable EE, any 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1, the corresponding threshold-based test has Type-I error guarantee α\alpha, i.e. for all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0},

P⁡(E≥1/α)≤α.P(E\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha. (3)
Proof.

(of Proposition 1) Markov’s inequality gives P⁡(E≥1/α)≤α​𝐄P​[E]≤αP(E\geq 1/\alpha)\leq\alpha\mathbf{E}_{P}[E]\leq\alpha. ∎

While reciprocals of e-variables thus give a special type of conservative p-values, reciprocals of standard p-values satisfying (2) are by no means e-variables; if EE is an e-variable and p is a standard p-value, and they are calculated on the same data, then we will usually observe p≪1/E\text{\it p}\ll 1/E so with e-values we need more extreme data in order to reject the null (see Section 6 for a nuanced analysis and Section 7 for more on e-p conversions).

Combining 1. and 2.: Optional Continuation

Proposition 2 below shows that multiplying e-variables E(1),E(2),…E_{(1)},E_{(2)},\ldots for tests based on respective independent samples 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}, 𝐘(2),…\mathbf{Y}_{(2)},\ldots (with each 𝐘(j)\mathbf{Y}_{(j)} being the batch of outcomes for the jj-th test), gives rise to new e-variables, even if the decision whether or not to perform the test resulting in E(j)E_{(j)} was based on the value of earlier test outcomes E(j−1),E(j−2),…E_{(j-1)},E_{(j-2)},\ldots As a result (Corollary 1), the Type I-Error Guarantee (3) remains valid even under this ‘optional continuation’ of testing. Just as importantly, in contrast to p-values, e-variables satisfy an ‘optional continuation principle’: whether an observed e-value is valid or not does not depend on whether or not you would have performed an additional study and gathered additional evidence in situations that did not occur.

An indication that something like this might be true is immediate from our gambling interpretation: if we start by investing $1 in E(1)E_{(1)} and, after observing E(1)E_{(1)}, reinvest all our new capital $E(1)\$E_{(1)} into E(2)E_{(2)}, then after observing E(2)E_{(2)} our new capital will obviously be $E(1)⋅E(2)\$E_{(1)}\cdot E_{(2)}, and so on. If, under the null, we do not expect to gain any money for any of the individual gambles E(j)E_{(j)}, then, intuitively, we should not expect to gain any money under whichever strategy we employ for deciding whether or not to reinvest (just as you would not expect to gain any money in a casino irrespective of your rule for re-investing and/or stopping and going home).

3. Third Interpretation: Bayes Factors

For convenience, from now on we write the models ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} as ℋ0={Pθ:θ∈Θ0};ℋ1={Pθ:θ∈Θ1},\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{0}\}\ \ ;\ \ \mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\}, where Θ0,Θ1⊂Θ\Theta_{0},\Theta_{1}\subset\Theta, and {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} represents a general family of distributions or random processes, defined relative to some given sample space and σ\sigma-algebra or filtration. 𝐘=YN=(Y1,…,YN)\mathbf{Y}=Y^{N}=(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{N}), a vector of NN outcomes, represents our data. NN may be a fixed sample size nn but can also be a random stopping time. We assume that, under every PθP_{\theta} with θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, 𝐘\mathbf{Y} has a probability density pθp_{\theta} relative to some fixed underlying measure μ\mu. In the Bayes factor approach to testing, one associates both ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} with a prior WjW_{j}, which is simply a probability distribution on Θj\Theta_{j}, and a Bayes marginal probability distribution PWj{P}_{W_{j}}, with density (or mass) function given by

pWj​(𝐘)≔∫Θjpθ​(𝐘)​d​Wj​(θ).{p}_{{\text{\tiny$W_{j}$}}}(\mathbf{Y})\coloneqq\int_{\Theta_{j}}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y})\,\textnormal{d}W_{j}(\theta). (4)

The Bayes factor is then given as:

𝖡𝖥≔pW1​(𝐘)pW0​(𝐘).\mathsf{BF}\coloneqq\frac{{p}_{{\text{\tiny$W_{1}$}}}(\mathbf{Y})}{{p}_{{\text{\tiny$W_{0}$}}}(\mathbf{Y})}. (5)

Whenever ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} is simple, i.e., a singleton, then the Bayes factor is also a (sharp, i.e. with expectation exactly 1) e-variable, since we must then have that W0W_{0} is degenerate, putting all mass on 00, and pW0=p0{p}_{\text{\tiny$W_{0}$}}=p_{0}, and then for all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, i.e. for P0P_{0}, we have, assuming P0P_{0} has strictly positive density,

𝐄P​[𝖡𝖥]=∫p0​(y)⋅pW1​(y)p0​(y)​d​μ​(y)=1.\mathbf{E}_{P}[\mathsf{BF}]=\int p_{0}(y)\cdot\frac{{p}_{{\text{\tiny$W_{1}$}}}(y)}{{p}_{0}(y)}\,\textnormal{d}\mu(y)=1. (6)

For such e-variables that are really simple-ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}-based Bayes factors, Proposition 1 reduces to the well-known universal bound for likelihood ratios (Royall, 1997). When ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is itself composite, most Bayes factors 𝖡𝖥=pW1/pW0\mathsf{BF}=p_{W_{1}}/p_{W_{0}} will not be e-variables any more, since for 𝖡𝖥\mathsf{BF} to be an e-variable we require (6) to hold for all Pθ,θ∈Θ0P_{\theta},\theta\in\Theta_{0}, whereas in general it only holds for P=PW0P=P_{W_{0}}. Nevertheless, Theorem 1 (in its first, simplest version in Section 2) implies that, under weak conditions, for every prior W1W_{1} on Θ1\Theta_{1} there always exists a corresponding prior W0W_{0} on Θ0\Theta_{0}, for which 𝖡𝖥=pW1/pW0\mathsf{BF}=p_{W_{1}}/p_{W_{0}} is an e-variable after all. More generally, in all our examples e-variables invariably take on a Bayesian form, though sometimes with highly unusual (e.g. degenerate) priors.

1.2 This Paper: Beyond Simple Nulls, Beyond Available Priors

In this paper, we focus on general, composite ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. The only assumption on ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is the existence of densities as above — we make this assumption because it allows for a completely general characterisation of GRO (‘growth-rate optimal’) e-variables as in Theorem 1. Still, useful e-variables for nonparametric settings without densities do exist (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2021, Orabona and Jun, 2021).

Theorem 1 in its first form in Section 2 tells us how to choose an e-variable that is optimal in the GRO sense if a prior W1W_{1} on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is given. Roughly speaking, GRO means that the e-variable tends to grow fast under ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} as more data come in, thereby generating substantial evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. The generalisations of Section 3–4, extend the GRO idea to e-variables when no such prior is available. Section 3 deals with a basic maximin optimality approach, which is appropriate if there is a single parameter of interest, a minimum relevant effect size, and no nuisance parameter. Section 4 describes relative maximin optimal e-variables, appropriate if there is no minimal effect size and/or nuisance parameters are present. This culminates in the fully general version of Theorem 1 in Section 4.3 which is also applicable to hypotheses with nuisance parameters that satisfy a group invariance, such as in the tt-test. To show that the e-variable we propose for the tt-test is indeed optimal we need a special case of an additional result, Theorem 4.2 of the paper (Perez et al., 2022), which, for convenience, we restate. But before embarking on these results, we explain the benefits of e-variable based tests in detail.

1.3 Optional Continuation

We defined e-variables for a single experiment. We now discuss sequential experimentation and how e-values can be combined to accumulate evidence against the null. To this end, let us imagine a sequence of random variables 𝐘(1),𝐘(2),…\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\mathbf{Y}_{(2)},\ldots representing the outcomes of experiments/studies. We will not (except for illustration purposes later on) make use of any internal structure of the 𝐘(j)\mathbf{Y}_{(j)}, which in particular may come to us as batches of varying lengths.

Definition 1.

Let ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} be a collection of distributions for a sample space equipped with filtration (ℱ(m))m(\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m}. We say that E(m)E_{(m)} is a ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-conditional e-variable (relative to null hypothesis ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}) if it is a nonnegative random variable that is ℱ(m)\mathcal{F}_{(m)}-measurable and for all P∈ℋ0:𝐄P[E(m)∣ℱ(m−1)]≤1a.s.\text{for all $P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}$:}\ \ {\bf E}_{P}[E_{(m)}\mid\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}]\leq 1\;\text{a.s.}. If, for each mm, E(m)E_{(m)} is an ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-conditional e-variable, we will call {E(m)}m\{E_{(m)}\}_{m} a conditional e-variable collection relative to (ℱ(m))m(\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m} .

In standard cases, ℱ(m)\mathcal{F}_{(m)} represent all that is known to us at time mm (that is, after having observed the mm-th study). Then it is simply σ⁡(𝐘(m))\sigma(\mathbf{Y}^{(m)}), with 𝐘(m)=(𝐘(1),…,𝐘(m))\mathbf{Y}^{(m)}=(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m)}) the sequence of outcomes of previous studies, and we could then rewrite the expectation elementarily as 𝐄P​[E(m)∣𝐘(m−1)]{\bf E}_{P}[E_{(m)}\mid{\bf Y}^{(m-1)}]. More generally though, ℱ(m)\mathcal{F}_{(m)} is allowed to be a coarser filtration as well: as long as for all mm, E(m)E_{(m)} is ℱ(m)\mathcal{F}_{(m)}-measurable, we can safely engage in optional continuation in the sense of Corollary 1 below, as explained in Section 5. On the other hand, ℱ(m)\mathcal{F}_{(m)} could also be finer, including nonstochastic side information such as ‘there is money to do an additional study’ or covariates; we briefly describe such extensions, as well as subtleties that may arise, in Appendix B.1.

Intuitively, ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-conditional e-values measure the conditional evidence in round mm (representing the mm-th study) against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, and hence their running product measures the total evidence (such a running product would then be a test super-martingale (Shafer et al., 2011), i.e. a nonnegative super-martingale with starting value ≤1\leq 1, under every element of the null). We may turn this running product into one quantity by adding a stopping rule. The following result, both parts of which are a direct implication of Doob’s optional stopping theorem (Williams, 1991) states that, irrespective of the stopping rule/time, we obtain a fair measure of evidence.

Proposition 2.
  1. 1.

    Let {E(m)}m\{E_{(m)}\}_{m} be a collection of conditional e-variables relative to filtration (ℱ(m))m\mathcal{(}\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m}. Then the running product (E(m))m(E^{(m)})_{m} with E(m):=∏j=1mE(j)E^{(m)}:=\prod_{j=1}^{m}E_{(j)} is a test super-martingale w.r.t. each P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}.

  2. 2.

    Any process (E(m))m(E^{(m)})_{m} that is a test super-martingale w.r.t. each P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0} is also an e-process (Ramdas et al., 2021) w.r.t. each P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, which by definition means that for any stopping time τ\tau (not necessarily finite), the stopped value E(τ)E^{(\tau)} is a (standard non-conditional) e-value for ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}.

Proposition 2 says that, no matter when we stop collecting batches of data, the resulting product is an e-variable and therefore a test based on it preserves Type-I error guarantees by Proposition 1. We note that, after the first version of the present paper appeared on arxiv, it was found that for some composite ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} there exist useful e-processes that are not test-martingales (Ramdas et al., 2021); we cannot build these as products of the conditional e-variables that our main theorem, presented in the next section, generates. On the other hand, as a referee suggested, in our optional continuation context the use of conditional e-variables as basic building blocks may also have advantages over general e-processes (for example, it is easier to switch (Erven et al., 2012) to a different type of e-variable from one study to the next); sorting this out in detail remains a question for future work.

Just-in-Time Conditional e-variables: Optional Continuation

As we can see from Proposition 2, the stopped running product E(τ)E^{(\tau)} of a sequence of conditional e-variables only evaluates each member variable E(m)E_{(m)} after mm rounds, and only on the data 𝐘(1),…,𝐘(m){\bf Y}_{(1)},\ldots,{\bf Y}_{(m)} that actually happened. It is therefore perfectly fine (for the Type-I error safety guaranteed by combining Propositions 2 and 1) for us to construct E(m)E_{(m)} on demand just before round mm, as a function of all available information so far (including possibly both stochastically modeled and arbitrary variables), as long as we ensure the conditional safety property in Definition 1. This simple observation gives us tremendous flexibility for testing, much in contrast to traditional p-values where the sampling plan needs to be fixed up front. In particular, it allows optional continuation: the practice of deciding after an initial series of experiments whether to output the current accumulated evidence, or perform yet more experiments.

Proposition 2 already indicates that we can safely engage in such optional continuation, assuming that we stop performing studies at some stopping time τ\tau relative to the filtration (ℱ(m))(m)(\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{(m)}. The following proposition expresses that we have Type-I error safety under optional continuation in an even stronger filtration-independent sense:

Corollary 1.

(of Proposition 2): “Ville-Robbins”

For all P∈ℋ0, all 0<α≤1:P(there exists m such that E(m)≥1α)≤α.\text{For all $P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}$, all $0<\alpha\leq 1$:}\ \ P\left(\text{there exists $m$ such that\ }E^{(m)}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\leq\alpha. (7)
Proof.

Proposition 2 expresses that E(1),E(2),…E^{(1)},E^{(2)},\ldots is a super-martingale with starting value ≤1\leq 1. Ville’s inequality (Ville, 1939) (also known as Ville-Robbins or Ville-Robbins-Wald inequality) then implies (7). ∎

For use later on, we formally define a threshold test based on non-negative process (E(m))m(E^{(m)})_{m} to be the random function that, when input mm and level α\alpha, outputs reject if E(m)≥1/αE^{(m)}\geq 1/\alpha and outputs accept otherwise (in this general definition, E(m)E^{(m)} can but does not need to be defined as a product of conditional e-variables). We say that a threshold test is safe under optional continuation with respect to Type I error if (7) holds. Thus, no matter when the data collecting and combination process is stopped, the Type-I error probability is preserved. We relate optional continuation to the more common notion of ‘optional stopping’ and discuss filtration-related subtleties in Section 5.

Whereas Ville-Robbins stresses that we may greedily ‘keep combining studies until we can reject or resources run out’, it is just as important that our e-values keep providing valid Type-I error guarantees if the continuation rule is externally imposed or unknowable.

Example 1.

Consider the simple scenario with a single underlying data stream Y1,Y2,…Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots with YiY_{i} i.i.d. according to both ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. Assume for simplicity simple ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} so that Bayes factors provide e-variables. For arbitrary prior WW on Θ1\Theta_{1}, define en,W​(Yn)=pW​(Yn)/p0​(Yn)e_{n,W}(Y^{n})=p_{W}(Y^{n})/p_{0}(Y^{n}) to be the Bayes factor as in (5) with prior WW for Θ1\Theta_{1} applied to data YnY^{n}.

Suppose we perform an initial study on sample 𝐘(1)≔YN(1)≔(Y1,…,YN(1))\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}\coloneqq Y^{N_{(1)}}\coloneqq(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{N_{(1)}}) and we equip Θ1\Theta_{1} with prior W(1)W_{(1)}. We can use as our e-variable E(1)E_{(1)} the Bayes factor E(1):=eN(1),W(1)​(𝐘(1))E_{(1)}:=e_{N_{(1)},W_{(1)}}(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}). Suppose this leads to a first e-value E(1)=18E_{(1)}=18 — promising enough for us to invest our resources into a subsequent study. We decide to gather N(2)N_{(2)} data points leading to data 𝐘(2)=(YN(1)+1,…,YN(1)+N(2))\mathbf{Y}_{(2)}=(Y_{N_{(1)}+1},\ldots,Y_{N_{(1)}+N_{(2)}}). For this second data batch, we will use an e-variable E(2)≔eN(2),W(2)​(𝐘(𝟐))E_{(2)}\coloneqq e_{N_{(2)},W_{(2)}}({\bf Y_{(2)}}) for a new prior W(2)W_{(2)}. Crucially, we are allowed to choose both N(2)N_{(2)} and W(2)W_{(2)} as a function of past data 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}^{(1)}: clearly, because the underlying data stream was assumed i.i.d., 𝐄P0​[E(2)∣𝐘(1)]≤1\mathbf{E}_{P_{0}}[E_{(2)}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}]\leq 1 irrespective of our choice (here we use (6)), and this allows us to use Proposition 2. If we want to stick to the Bayesian paradigm, we can choose W(2)≔W(1)(⋅∣𝐘(1))W_{(2)}\coloneqq{W_{(1)}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{Y}_{(1)})}, as the Bayes posterior for θ1\theta_{1} based on data 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)} and prior W(1)W_{(1)}. Bayes’ theorem shows that multiplying E(2)≔E(1)⋅E(2)E^{(2)}\coloneqq E_{(1)}\cdot E_{(2)} (which gives a new e-variable by Proposition 2), satisfies

E(2)=E(1)⋅E(2)=pW(1)(𝐘(1))⋅pW(1)(⋅∣𝐘(1))(𝐘(2))p0​(𝐘(1))⋅p0​(𝐘(2))=pW(1)​(Y1,…,YN(2))p0​(Y1,…,YN(2)),E^{(2)}=E_{(1)}\cdot E_{(2)}=\frac{{p}_{W_{(1)}}(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)})\cdot{p}_{W_{(1)}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{Y}_{(1)})}(\mathbf{Y}_{(2)})}{p_{0}(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)})\cdot p_{0}(\mathbf{Y}_{(2)})}=\frac{{p}_{W_{(1)}}(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{N_{(2)}})}{p_{0}(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{N_{(2)}})}, (8)

which is exactly what one would get by Bayesian updating. This illustrates that, for simple ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, combining e-variables by multiplication can be done consistently with Bayesian updating.

The Local Perspective

It might also be the case that it is not us who get the additional funding to obtain extra data, but rather some research group at a different location. If the question is, say, whether a medication works, the null hypothesis would still be ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} but, if it works, its effectiveness might be slightly different due to slight differences in population. In that case, the research group might decide to use a different test statistic E(2)′E^{\prime}_{(2)} which is again a Bayes factor, but now with an alternative prior WW on θ1\theta_{1} (for example, the original prior W(1)W_{(1)} might be re-used rather than replaced by W(1)(⋅∣𝐘(1))W_{(1)}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{Y}_{(1)})) — one might call this the local perspective. Even though not standard Bayesian, E(1)⋅E(2)′E_{(1)}\cdot E^{\prime}_{(2)} still gives a valid e-variable, and Type-I error guarantees are preserved — and the same will hold even if the new research group would use an entirely different prior on Θ1\Theta_{1}. And, after the second batch of data 𝐘(2)\mathbf{Y}_{(2)}, one might consider obtaining even more samples, each time using a different W(j)W_{(j)}, that is always allowed to depend on the past in arbitrary ways.

Finally, it is important to note that, when combining studies, we do require all the data batches 𝐘(1),𝐘(2),…\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\mathbf{Y}_{(2)},\ldots to refer to separate data: obviously it is not allowed to ‘borrow’ some data from 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)} and reuse it as part of 𝐘(2)\mathbf{Y}_{(2)}. E-values based partly on the same data can still be validly combined (e.g. by averaging (Vovk and Wang, 2021)) but not by multiplication as we do here.

2 The GRO e-Variable

Mathematical Preliminaries

In this and the coming sections we present our main result, Theorem 1. We first list all required mathematical notations and definitions. We invariably assume that some family {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} of probability distributions for 𝒴\mathcal{Y} has been fixed and all PθP_{\theta} with θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta have densities relative to some underlying measure μ\mu. When we write ‘pp is a (sub-) probability density’, we mean it is a (sub-) probability density relative to μ\mu, i.e. p≥0p\geq 0 and ∫p⁡(𝐘)​𝑑μ=1\int p(\mathbf{Y})d\mu=1 for a density and ∫p⁡(𝐘)​𝑑μ≤1\int p(\mathbf{Y})d\mu\leq 1 for a sub-density. In the latter case we call the measure PP with density pp a sub-probability distribution. We use D(Q∥P)D(Q\|P) to denote the Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence between distributions QQ and PP (Cover and Thomas, 1991). We allow PP (but not QQ) to be a sub-probability distribution, with D(Q∥P)=𝐄𝐘∼Q[lnq(𝐘)/p(𝐘)]D(Q\|P)={\bf E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim Q}[\ln q(\mathbf{Y})/p(\mathbf{Y})]. We say that random variables U∗U^{*} and U∘U^{\circ} are essentially equal if, for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, Pθ​(U∗=U∘)=1P_{\theta}(U^{*}=U^{\circ})=1. We say that U∗U^{*} essentially uniquely satisfies property prop if all other random variables satisfying property prop are essentially equal to U∗U^{*}. When we write ‘PP has full support’, we mean that its density pp satisfies p⁡(𝐘)>0p({\bf Y})>0 μ\mu-almost everywhere. We assume some suitable σ\sigma-algebra including all singleton sets on Θ\Theta has been defined, and for Θ′⊂Θ\Theta^{\prime}\subset\Theta we let 𝒲⁡(Θ′)\mathcal{W}(\Theta^{\prime}) be the set of all probability distributions (i.e., ‘proper priors’) on Θ′\Theta^{\prime} with this σ\sigma-algebra. Notably, 𝒲⁡(Θ′)\mathcal{W}(\Theta^{\prime}) includes, for each θ∈Θ′\theta\in\Theta^{\prime}, the degenerate distribution WW which puts all mass on θ\theta. We say that WW essentially uniquely satisfies property prop among 𝒲⁡(Θ′)\mathcal{W}(\Theta^{\prime}) if for all other distributions W′∈𝒲⁡(Θ′)W^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta^{\prime}) that satisfy prop and all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, we have Pθ​(pW=pW′)=1P_{\theta}(p_{W}=p^{\prime}_{W})=1, where pWp_{W} and pW′p^{\prime}_{W} are as in (4). ℰ⁡(Θ0)\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0}) is defined as the set of all e-variables that can be defined on 𝐘\mathbf{Y} for Θ0\Theta_{0}, i.e. all random variables satisfying (1). We frequently use the fact that if Θ0={0}\Theta_{0}=\{0\} is a singleton so that ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is simple, then the class of e-variables corresponds exactly to the set of likelihood ratios relative to p0p_{0}:

ℰ⁡({0})={q⁡(𝐘)p0​(𝐘):q is a sub-probability density for 𝐘}.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\{0\})=\left\{\frac{q(\mathbf{Y})}{p_{0}(\mathbf{Y})}\;:\text{$q$ is a sub-probability density for $\mathbf{Y}$}\;\right\}. (9)

To see this, note that for every e-variable E=e⁡(𝐘)E=e({\bf Y)} we can define q⁡(𝐘):=e⁡(𝐘)⋅p0​(𝐘)q({\bf Y}):=e({\bf Y})\cdot p_{0}({\bf Y}) and then ∫q​𝑑μ=∫p0​(𝐘)​e​(𝐘)​𝑑μ≤1\int qd\mu=\int p_{0}({\bf Y})e({\bf Y})d\mu\leq 1; conversely every sub-density qq defines an e-variable by setting E=q⁡(𝐘)/p0​(𝐘)E=q({\bf Y})/p_{0}({\bf Y}) which gives 𝐄P0​[E]≤1\mathbf{E}_{P_{0}}[E]\leq 1.

Our main theorem (proof in Appendix A.1) implies that nontrivial e-variables exist without any further conditions:

Theorem 1.

Suppose QQ is a probability distribution with full support and with density qq, and assume infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)<∞\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})<\infty. Then there exists a (potentially sub-) distribution P0∗P^{*}_{0} with density p0∗p^{*}_{0} such that

E∗:=q⁡(𝐘)p0∗​(𝐘)E^{*}:=\frac{q(\mathbf{Y})}{p^{*}_{0}(\mathbf{Y})} (10)

is an e-variable. Moreover, E∗E^{*} satisfies, essentially uniquely,

supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)𝐄𝐘∼Q[logE]=𝐄𝐘∼Q[logE∗]=infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)=D(Q∥P0∗).\displaystyle\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim Q}[\log E]=\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim Q}[\log E^{*}]=\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})=D(Q\|P^{*}_{0}). (11)

If the minimum is achieved by some W0∗{W}^{*}_{0}, i.e. D(Q∥P0∗)=D(Q∥PW0∗)D(Q\|P^{*}_{0})=D(Q\|P_{W^{*}_{0}}), then P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W^{*}_{0}}.

The full support condition is natural and discussed further in Appendix A.3. Following Barron and Li (1999) (see also (Csiszár and Matus, 2003)), we call P0∗P^{*}_{0} the Reverse Information Projection (RIPr) of QQ on 𝒫⁡(Θ0)={PW0:W0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)}{\cal P}(\Theta_{0})=\{P_{W_{0}}:W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})\}. In all examples in this paper, we have P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W^{*}_{0}}: the minimum is achieved and its density integrates to 11 (one can construct special ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} for which p0∗p^{*}_{0} integrates to strictly less than 11 (Harremoës, 2021), but we do not know whether this happens for any practically relevant ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}). The following corollary (see Appendix A.1 for details) is useful in applications:

Corollary 2.

E∗E^{*} is the only e-variable of Bayes factor/likelihood ratio form with qq in the numerator. That is, for all W0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}): if PW0P_{W_{0}} is not essentially equal to P0∗P^{*}_{0} then q​(𝐘)/pW0​(𝐘)q(\mathbf{Y})/p_{W_{0}}(\mathbf{Y}) is not an e-variable. In particular this implies: (a) if P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W^{*}_{0}}, then W0∗W^{*}_{0} achieves minW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)\min_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}}) essentially uniquely; and (b) if we have found an e-variable of form q​(𝐘)/pW0​(𝐘)q(\mathbf{Y})/p_{W_{0}}(\mathbf{Y}) then W0W_{0} must be essentially equal to W0∗W^{*}_{0}.

Theorem 1 leaves open the question of how to calculate W0∗W^{*}_{0}, if it exists. In the examples we encounter below, we can either show that W0∗W^{*}_{0} is degenerate, putting all its mass on a single distribution Pθ0∗P_{\theta^{*}_{0}}, and θ0∗\theta^{*}_{0} can be determined analytically, or, as in the t-test example, we can analytically find it by other means. ‘Easy’ W0∗W^{*}_{0} occur in surprisingly many other situations as well (see e.g. (ter Schure et al., 2021, Koolen and Grünwald, 2021)), but by no means always (Adams, 2020). More generally, even if W0∗W^{*}_{0} is not easy to determine analytically, as long as 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is finite then, using Carathéodory’s theorem we can still show that W0∗W^{*}_{0} must exist and has finite support. By strict convexity of KL divergence in its second argument it can therefore in principle be found by numerical methods, but more research is needed to see existing methods are fast enough in practice. If 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is infinite, one can still try to approximate W0∗W^{*}_{0} numerically but it may be hard to determine the accuracy of such approximations.

2.1 The GRO criterion when ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is simple

We now focus on the case with a given alternative ℋ1={Pθ:θ∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\}, and for now assume Θ1={θ1}\Theta_{1}=\{\theta_{1}\} is a singleton. Applying Theorem 1 above with Q=Pθ1Q=P_{\theta_{1}}, we call the resulting E∗E^{*} (or any essentially equal version of it) the θ1\theta_{1}-GRO e-variable, GRO standing for growth-rate optimal. We define the growth rate achievable with θ1\theta_{1} as

GRO(θ1):=supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)𝐄Y∼Pθ1[logE]=D(Pθ1∥P0∗),\text{GRO}(\theta_{1}):=\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}{\bf E}_{Y\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E]=D(P_{\theta_{1}}\|P^{*}_{0}), (12)

with the equality following from Theorem 1 (we omit Θ0\Theta_{0} in the notations since, in contrast to Θ1\Theta_{1} or θ1\theta_{1}, Θ0\Theta_{0} will always be clear from context). In general, there exist many nontrivial e-variables for a given ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. The θ1\theta_{1}-GRO e-variable is a special one that is optimal in a natural sense for the given ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}: whereas in the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, one measures the quality of a test at a given significance level α\alpha by its power, i.e. the probability of correct decision under θ1\theta_{1}, we will measure it by the expected capital growth rate under θ1\theta_{1}. This is different from power, yet there are close connections to which we return in Section 9.

To explain, we return to the monetary interpretation of e-values. The definition of e-variable ensures that we expect them to stay under 11 (one does not gain money) under any P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}. Analogously, one would like them to be constructed such that they can be expected to grow large as fast as possible (one gets rich, gets evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}) under ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. Assuming for now that ℋ1={Pθ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta_{1}}\} is simple, this suggests to define the optimal e-variable E∗E^{*} as the one that maximises 𝐄Pθ1​[f⁡(E∗)]\mathbf{E}_{P_{\theta_{1}}}[f(E^{*})] for some function that is increasing in E∗E^{*}. At first sight it may seem natural to pick ff the identity, but this can lead to adoption of an e-variable E∗E^{*} such that Pθ1​(E∗=0)>0P_{\theta_{1}}(E^{*}=0)>0. This choice, however, does not go together well with preserving evidence (capital) under optional continuation: if E(1)∗E^{*}_{(1)} is 00 with positive probability, then it may happen that the evidence E(m)=∏j=1mE(j)E^{(m)}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}E_{(j)} obtained so far remains 00, no matter how large E(j)E_{(j)} for j≥1j\geq 1 — akin to losing all one’s money in the first round at a roulette table. A similar objection applies to any polynomial ff, but it does not apply to the logarithm, which is also the asymptotically optimal choice for ff if samples are independent: by Kolmogorov’s strong law of large numbers, any sequence of e-variables E(1),E(2),…E_{(1)},E_{(2)},\ldots based on independent 𝐘(1),𝐘(2),…\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\mathbf{Y}_{(2)},\ldots with supj∈ℕ𝐄𝐘(j)∼Pθ1​[(log⁡E(j))2]/(j/log2⁡(j+1))<∞\sup_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}_{(j)}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[(\log E_{(j)})^{2}]/(j/\log^{2}(j+1))<\infty (in particular this holds if the variances are uniformly bounded), will a.s. satisfy (1/m)​∑j=1m(log⁡E(j))−(1/m)​∑j=1m𝐄𝐘(j)∼Pθ1​[log⁡E(j)]→0(1/m)\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\log E_{(j)}\right)-(1/m)\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}_{(j)}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E_{(j)}]\rightarrow 0. Thus, E(m)≔∏j=1mE(j)E^{(m)}\coloneqq\prod_{j=1}^{m}E_{(j)} will grow exponentially fast if all 𝐄𝐘(j)∼Pθ1​[log⁡E(j)]>0\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}_{(j)}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E_{(j)}]>0, with maximal growth rate attained if the E(j)E_{(j)} are chosen to maximize 𝐄𝐘(j)∼Pθ1​[log⁡E(j)]\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}_{(j)}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E_{(j)}] — a quantity which, for log\log taken to the base 22, is known as the doubling rate (Cover and Thomas, 1991, Kelly, 1956). This provides a powerful reason for choosing the logarithm; see also the extensive exposition by Shafer (2021). We return to GRO’s motivation in Section 8.

Example 2.

[2×22\times 2 Contingency Tables] Let 𝒴n={0,1}n\mathcal{Y}^{n}=\{0,1\}^{n} and let 𝒳={a,b}\mathcal{X}=\{a,b\} represent two categories. We start with a multinomial model 𝒢\mathcal{G} on 𝒵=𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, extended to nn outcomes by independence. We want to test whether the YiY_{i} are dependent on the XiX_{i}. To this end, we condition every distribution in 𝒢\mathcal{G} on a fixed, given, Xn=𝐱X^{n}=\mathbf{x} with 𝐱=(x1,…,xn)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), and we let ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} be the set of (or a subset of the) conditional distributions on 𝒵\mathcal{Z} that thus result. We thus assume the design of 𝒳n\mathcal{X}^{n} to be set in advance, but N1N_{1}, the number of ones, to be random; alternative choices are possible and would lead to a different analysis. Conditioned on Xn=𝐱X^{n}=\mathbf{x}, the likelihood of an individual sequence 𝐲|𝐱\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x} becomes:

pμ1|a,μ1|b​(𝐲∣𝐱)=μ1|ana​1​(1−μ1|a)na​0⋅μ1|bnb​1​(1−μ1|b)nb​0,\displaystyle p_{\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})=\mu_{1|a}^{n_{a1}}(1-\mu_{1|a})^{n_{a0}}\cdot\mu_{1|b}^{n_{b1}}(1-\mu_{1|b})^{n_{b0}}, (13)

where nj​in_{ji} is the number of times outcome ii was observed to fall in category jj and μ1|j\mu_{1|j} is the probability of observing a 11 given category jj. These densities define the full model {Pμ1|a,μ1|b:(μ1|a,μ1|b)∈Θ}\{P_{\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}}:(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})\in\Theta\} with Θ=[0,1]2\Theta=[0,1]^{2}. ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, the null model, simply has (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}) and 𝐘=(Y1,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}) independent, with Yi,…,YnY_{i},\ldots,Y_{n} i.i.d. Ber​(μ)\text{Ber}(\mu) distributed, μ∈Θ0≔[0,1]\mu\in\Theta_{0}\coloneqq[0,1], i.e. pμ​(𝐲∣𝐱)=pμ​(𝐲)=μn1​(1−μ)n−n1p_{\mu}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})=p_{\mu}(\mathbf{y})=\mu^{n_{1}}(1-\mu)^{n-n_{1}} with n1=na​1+nb​1n_{1}=n_{a1}+n_{b1}. We defer description of the test of the full alternative {Pθ:θ∈Θ1}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\} with Θ1=(0,1)2\Theta_{1}=(0,1)^{2} against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} to Section 4.1. For now, we assume a simple ℋ1={Pθ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta_{1}}\} for a specific θ1=(μ1|a,μ1|b)\theta_{1}=(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}) with μ1|a≠μ1|b\mu_{1|a}\neq\mu_{1|b}. Turner et al. (2021) shows that the RIPr for Pθ1P_{\theta_{1}}, achieving the infimum in (11) is given by P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W^{*}_{0}} where W0∗W^{*}_{0} is the degenerate prior that puts all its mass on the single point μ∘=(na​μ1|a+nb​μ1|b)/(na+nb)\mu^{\circ}=(n_{a}\mu_{1|a}+n_{b}\mu_{1|b})/(n_{a}+n_{b}). Thus, the θ1\theta_{1}-GRO e-variable has an intuitive form here, being given by

E∗=pμ1|a,μ1|b​(𝐘∣𝐱)pμ∘​(𝐘∣𝐱).\displaystyle E^{*}=\frac{p_{\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}}({\bf Y}\mid{\bf x})}{p_{\mu^{\circ}}({\bf Y}\mid{\bf x})}. (14)

The fact that the RIPr is achieved by a point prior is quite specific to contingency tables. We also note that, while the expectation of E∗E^{*} is bounded by 11 under all Pμ∈ℋ0P_{\mu}\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, its actual distribution function varies with PμP_{\mu}. This is in contrast to the t-test example, in which the GRO E∗E^{*} turns out to have the same distribution under all distributions in the null.

2.2 GRO when prior on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is available

We now take a Bayesian stance regarding ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and, conditioned on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, are prepared to represent our uncertainty by prior distribution W1W_{1} on Θ1\Theta_{1}. The marginal distribution of 𝐘\bf Y is then PW1​(𝐘)P_{W_{1}}(\bf Y). Applying Theorem 1 with PW1P_{W_{1}} as QQ then leads to the “W1W_{1}-GRO e-variable” — it would be optimal in the GRO sense under prior W1W_{1}. This e-variable is a Bayes factor, but gives only a quasi-Bayesian notion of evidence since any prior W1W_{1} on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} that we wish to adopt forces us to adopt a particular corresponding prior W0∗∈ℋ0W^{*}_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{0}. One may perhaps consider this a small price to pay for creating a Bayes factor that, by its Type-I error safety under optional continuation, should be acceptable to frequentists as well. Moreover it is often recognised that priors on Θ0\Theta_{0} and Θ1\Theta_{1} should somehow be ‘matched’ to each other (Berger et al., 1998); we may view the RIPr construction as providing a reasonable (from a frequentist stance) matching.

Example 3.

[Gaussian Location with Gaussian prior (z-test)] Now consider ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} according to which the YiY_{i} are i.i.d. ∼N⁡(μ,1)\sim N(\mu,1) for some μ∈Θ1=ℝ\mu\in\Theta_{1}=\mathbb{R}, so that pμ(𝐘)=pμ(Y1,…,Yn)∝exp(−∑i=1n(Yi−μ)2/2)p_{\mu}(\mathbf{Y})=p_{\mu}(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})\propto\exp(-\sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_{i}-\mu)^{2}/2). We let ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\}. We perform a Bayes factor test using E:=pW​(𝐘)/p0​(𝐘)E:=p_{W}(\mathbf{Y})/p_{0}(\mathbf{Y}) where we take the prior WW to have Gaussian density w(μ)∝exp(−μ2/2)w(\mu)\propto\exp(-\mu^{2}/2). By (6) we know that EE is not just a Bayes factor but also an e-variable. By straightforward calculation:

−12​log⁡(n+1)+12​(n+1)⋅μ˘n2,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\log(n+1)+\frac{1}{2}(n+1)\cdot\breve{\mu}_{n}^{2},

where μ˘n=(∑i=1Yi)/(n+1)\breve{\mu}_{n}=(\sum_{i=1}Y_{i})/(n+1) is the Bayes MAP estimator, which only differs from the ML estimator by O⁡(1/n2)O(1/n^{2}): μ˘n−μ^n=μ^n/(n⁡(n+1))\breve{\mu}_{n}-\hat{\mu}_{n}=\hat{\mu}_{n}/(n(n+1)). If we were to reject Θ0\Theta_{0} when E≥20E\geq 20 (giving, by Proposition 1 a Type-I error guarantee of 0.050.05), we would thus reject if

|μ˘n|≥5.99+log⁡(n+1)n+1, i.e. ​|μ^n|⪰(log⁡n)/n,|\breve{\mu}_{n}|\geq\sqrt{\frac{5.99+\log(n+1)}{n+1}},\text{\ i.e.\ }|\hat{\mu}_{n}|\succeq\sqrt{(\log n)/n}, (15)

where we used 2​log⁡20≈5.992\log 20\approx 5.99. Contrast this with the standard two-sided Neyman-Pearson (NP) test, which would reject (with α=0.05\alpha=0.05) if |μ^n|≥1.96/n|\hat{\mu}_{n}|\geq 1.96/\sqrt{n}, or the one-sided test which would reject if μ^n≥1.645/n\hat{\mu}_{n}\geq 1.645/\sqrt{n} or the e-value based tests of the next section: the standard Bayesian test is significantly more conservative, requiring more data to conclude rejection. In Section 6 we investigate this further.

3 The GROW e-Variable

We now show how to construct good e-variables if ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is composite and no prior on Θ1\Theta_{1} is available. We focus on variations of worst-case (maximin) growth optimality, but this is certainly not the only criterion that might be useful or valuable; see the discussion in Section 8. In the case of simple ℋ1={Pθ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta_{1}}\}, we aimed for e-variables that could be expected to grow as fast as possible under Pθ1P_{\theta_{1}}. Analogously, we would now like them to be constructed such that they can be expected to grow large as fast as possible (one gets rich, gets evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}) under all P1∈ℋ1P_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{1}. We call e-variables satisfying this property GROW: growth-rate optimal in worst-case. We now discuss the simplest, ‘raw’ form of this criterion — in some settings a modification of this criterion, REGROW, which we discuss in the next section, is more suitable. GROW tells us to pick, among all e-variables relative to ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, the E∗E^{*} that achieves the worst-case optimal expected capital growth rate

GROW(Θ1):=supE:E∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)infθ∈Θ1𝐄Pθ[logE].\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1}):=\sup_{E:E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{P_{\theta}}\left[\log E\right]. (16)

Theorem 1, First Generalisation Suppose all Pθ,Pθ′P_{\theta},P_{\theta^{\prime}} with θ,θ′∈Θ1\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta_{1} satisfy D(Pθ∥Pθ′)<∞D(P_{\theta}\|P_{\theta^{\prime}})<\infty, and have full support. If infW1∈𝒲1,W0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW1∥PW0)=infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW1∗∥PW0)<∞,\inf_{W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}_{1},W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})=\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})<\infty, (i.e. the minimum on the left over 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1} is achieved by W1∗W^{*}_{1}) then then there exists an e-variable

E∗:=pW1∗​(𝐘)p0∗​(𝐘),E^{*}:=\frac{p_{W^{*}_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})}{p^{*}_{0}(\mathbf{Y})}, (17)

where p0∗p_{0}^{*} is the density of P0∗P^{*}_{0}, a (potentially sub-) distribution satisfying infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW1∗∥PW0)=D(PW1∗∥P0∗)\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})=D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P^{*}_{0}), and E∗E^{*} achieves (16), satisfying, essentially uniquely: infθ∈Θ1𝐄𝐘∼Pθ[logE∗]=supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)infθ∈Θ1𝐄𝐘∼Pθ[logE]=D(PW1∗∥P0∗).\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log E^{*}]=\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log E]=D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{*}_{0}). If further D(PW1∗∥P0∗)=D(PW1∗∥PW0∗)D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P^{*}_{0})=D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P_{W_{0}^{*}}) for some W0∗∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)W_{0}^{*}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}), then P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W_{0}^{*}}.

The earlier version of Theorem 1 is the special case we get if we set Θ1={θ1}\Theta_{1}=\{\theta_{1}\} a singleton and Q:=Pθ1Q:=P_{\theta_{1}}. This generalized version expresses that the GROW e-variable is once again a Bayes factor — a special one in fact, between the components of the joint information projection (PW1∗,P0∗)(P_{W_{1}^{*}},P^{*}_{0}) (Csiszár and Tusnády, 1984); see Figure 1. As to computing W1∗W^{*}_{1} in practice, the same remarks apply as we already made (underneath Corollary 2) regarding computing W0∗W^{*}_{0}.

3.1 One-parameter models with minimum relevant effect size

Let Θ\Theta be a connected subset of ℝ\mathbb{R} indexing a 1-parameter parametric model {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} with θ\theta indicating the size of some effect. If, as is standard practice in e.g. medical statistics, we have a minimum clinically relevant effect size δ+\delta^{+} and a status quo δ−<δ+\delta^{-}<\delta^{+} in mind, we want to test

Θ0={θ∈Θ:θ≤δ−}​ vs. ​Θ1={θ∈Θ:θ≥δ+}.\Theta_{0}=\{\theta\in\Theta:\theta\leq\delta^{-}\}\text{\ vs.\ }\Theta_{1}=\{\theta\in\Theta:\theta\geq\delta^{+}\}. (18)

In standard cases, often δ−=0\delta^{-}=0 and Θ0:={0}\Theta_{0}:=\{0\}.

Proposition 3.

Suppose there exists a 1-dimensional statistic T=t⁡(𝐘)T=t({\bf Y}) such that the family of densities {pθ:θ∈Θ}\{p_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} has a monotone likelihood ratio in TT. Then for all δ−<δ+\delta^{-}<\delta^{+} with δ−,δ+∈Θ\delta^{-},\delta^{+}\in\Theta, the GROW e-variable relative to Θ1\Theta_{1} and Θ0\Theta_{0} as in (18), is given by E∗=pδ+​(𝐘)/pδ−​(𝐘)E^{*}=p_{\delta^{+}}({\bf Y})/p_{\delta^{-}}({\bf Y}): it sets W1∗W^{*}_{1} and W0∗W^{*}_{0} to be degenerate priors, putting all mass on δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-}, respectively.

We now illustrate Proposition 3 for 1-dimensional exponential families, but stress that it can be applied to some other families (e.g. location families or the t-test setting in Section 4.3) as well.

Example 4.

[GROW for 1-dimensional exponential families] Let {Pθ∣θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}\mid\theta\in\Theta\} represent a 1-parameter exponential family for sample space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, given in its mean-value parameterisation, where Θ\Theta is a connected subset of (and possibly equal to) the full mean-value parameter space. Let δ−<δ+\delta^{-}<\delta^{+} with δ−,δ+\delta^{-},\delta^{+} both in Θ\Theta. Both ℋ0={Pθ:θ∈Θ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{0}\} and ℋ1={Pθ:θ∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\} with Θ0,Θ1\Theta_{0},\Theta_{1} as in (18) are extended to outcomes in 𝐘=(Y1,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}) by independence. Let T=t⁡(𝐘)T=t({\bf Y}) be the sufficient statistic of the exponential family under consideration, i.e. 𝐄𝐘∼Pθ​[t​(𝐘)]=θ\mathbf{E}_{{\bf Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[t({\bf Y})]=\theta. It is well-known that the monotone likelihood property holds in the statistic TT. It thus follows from Proposition 3 above that the GROW e-variable relative to Θ1\Theta_{1} and Θ0\Theta_{0} can be calculated as a likelihood ratio E∗=pδ+​(𝐘)/pδ−​(𝐘)E^{*}=p_{\delta^{+}}(\mathbf{Y})/p_{\delta^{-}}(\mathbf{Y}) between two point hypotheses, even though Θ1\Theta_{1} and/or Θ0\Theta_{0} may be composite. Comparison of the ensuing test to the Neyman-Pearson and Bayes factor tests are given in Section 6.

4 The REGROW e-variable: general composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} case

Theorem 1, Further Generalisation Let f⁡(θ)f(\theta) be a function that is bounded on Θ1\Theta_{1}; we abbreviate f⁡(W):=𝐄θ∼W​[f⁡(θ)]f(W):=\mathbf{E}_{\theta\sim W}[f(\theta)]. Suppose all Pθ,Pθ′P_{\theta},P_{\theta^{\prime}} with θ,θ′∈Θ1\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta_{1} satisfy D(Pθ∥Pθ′)<∞D(P_{\theta}\|P_{\theta^{\prime}})<\infty, and have full support. If infW1∈𝒲⁡(Θ1),W0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)(D(PW1∥PW0)−f(W1))=infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW1∗∥PW0)−f(W1∗)<∞\inf_{W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}),W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}(D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})-f(W_{1}))=\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})-f(W^{*}_{1})<\infty then there exists an e-variable EfE^{f} given by

Ef:=pW1∗​(𝐘)p0∗​(𝐘)E^{f}:=\frac{p_{W^{*}_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})}{p^{*}_{0}(\mathbf{Y})} (19)

where p0∗p^{*}_{0} is the density of P0∗P^{*}_{0}, a (potentially sub-) distribution such that infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW1∗∥PW0)=D(PW1∗∥P0∗)\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})=D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P^{*}_{0}), and EfE^{f} satisfies, essentially uniquely:

infθ∈Θ1(𝐄𝐘∼Pθ[logEf]−f(θ))=supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)infθ∈Θ1(𝐄𝐘∼Pθ[logE]−f(θ))=D(PW1∗∥P0∗)−f(W1∗).\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log E^{f}]-f(\theta)\ )=\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log E]-f(\theta)\ )=D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{*}_{0})-f(W^{*}_{1}). (20)

If further D(PW1∗∥P0∗)=D(PW1∗∥PW0∗)D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P^{*}_{0})=D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P_{W_{0}^{*}}) for some W0∗∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)W_{0}^{*}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}), then P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W_{0}^{*}}.

We call EfE^{f} the REGROW (standing for relative growth in the worst-case) e-variable relative to offset ff. The previous version of Theorem 1 is the special case with ff constant. The offset ff will be useful when Θ0\Theta_{0} and Θ1\Theta_{1} are nested and no effect size can be stated in advance (Section 4.1) and/or when nuisance parameters are present (Section 4.2 and 4.3). All these cases can be handled essentially the same way (and we may in fact think of the case of nested models as a situation in which all parameters in Θ0\Theta_{0} are viewed as nuisance): we first consider a modified problem in which Θ1\Theta_{1} is reduced to a singleton. That is, we imagine that some oracle tells us “if ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is the case, then the data are sampled from this specific θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1}”. We then consider the corresponding GRO​(θ1∗)=GROW​({θ1∗})\text{GRO}(\theta^{*}_{1})=\text{GROW}(\{\theta^{*}_{1}\}) and view this as the desirable but unobtainable expected growth rate — the one we could have obtained if we had known θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1}. We may now aim for the e-variable such that, no matter what θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1} turns out to be, our expected growth is close to the optimum we could have obtained had we known θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1}. Thus, we want to be worst-case growth optimal relative to f(θ1):=GRO(θ1)=𝐄Pθ1[logEθ1∗]=infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Pθ1∥PW0)f(\theta_{1}):=\text{GRO}(\theta_{1})=\mathbf{E}_{P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E^{*}_{\theta_{1}}]=\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{\theta_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}}) (where we write Eθ1∗E^{*}_{\theta_{1}} for the GRO e-variable for testing {θ1}\{\theta_{1}\} vs. Θ0\Theta_{0} and the second equality follows by (12)). Plugging in this ff and taking negatives on both sides, (20) now becomes:

supθ1∈Θ1𝐄𝐘∼Pθ1​[log⁡Eθ1∗−log⁡Ef]=infE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)supθ1∈Θ1𝐄𝐘∼Pθ1​[log⁡Eθ1∗−log⁡E]=𝐄θ1∼W1∗[infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Pθ1∥PW0)]−D(PW1∗∥P∗0),\sup_{\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}\left[\log E^{*}_{\theta_{1}}-\log E^{f}\right]=\inf_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\sup_{\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E^{*}_{\theta_{1}}-\log E]=\\ \mathbf{E}_{\theta_{1}\sim W^{*}_{1}}\left[\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{\theta_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})\right]-D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{*}_{0}), (21)

an expression that is always nonnegative, since, by definition of Eθ1∗E^{*}_{\theta_{1}}, for any e-variable EE, 𝐄𝐘∼Pθ1​[log⁡Eθ1∗]≥𝐄𝐘∼Pθ1​[log⁡E]\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E^{*}_{\theta_{1}}]\geq\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta_{1}}}[\log E]. This shows that EfE^{f} can be thought of as a minimax pseudo-regret e-variable, regret being the loss of expected capital growth under ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} due to not knowing the underlying θ1\theta_{1} in advance.

4.1 Composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, no effect size known

Suppose we are interested in detecting whether there is any deviation at all from the null. There is no pre-stated effect size, and Θ0⊂Θ1=Θ\Theta_{0}\subset\Theta_{1}=\Theta are nested, or more generally, for all θ1∈Θ1\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1}, infθ0∈Θ0D(Pθ1∥Pθ0)=0\inf_{\theta_{0}\in\Theta_{0}}D(P_{\theta_{1}}\|P_{\theta_{0}})=0. In this case, GROW​(Θ1)=0\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1})=0 and the GROW e-variable that achieves it is equal to E∗=1E^{*}=1, which will never give any evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, so clearly, the raw GROW approach is not useful. Instead, in this setting, the REGROW approach is a sensible generalisation of successful existing approaches. We first establish this for simple nulls:

Simple Nulls

If Θ0={0}\Theta_{0}=\{0\} is simple, we have infW0D(Pθ1∥PW0)=D(Pθ1∥P0)\inf_{W_{0}}D(P_{\theta_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})=D(P_{\theta_{1}}\|P_{0}) and D(PW1∗∥PW0∗)=D(PW1∗∥P0)D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P_{W_{0}^{*}})=D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P_{0}), and terms in (21) involving −log⁡p0​(𝐘)-\log p_{0}(\mathbf{Y}) cancel. Further using the 1-to-1 mapping (9) between probability densities and e-variables for the case of point 00’s to rewrite (21) and using Ef=pW1∗​(𝐘)/p0​(𝐘)E^{f}=p_{W^{*}_{1}}({\bf Y})/p_{0}({\bf Y}), (21) simplifies to:

supθ∈Θ1𝐄𝐘∼Pθ[−logpW1∗​(𝐘)pθ​(𝐘)]=infqsupθ∈Θ1𝐄𝐘∼Pθ[−logq⁡(𝐘)pθ​(𝐘)]=supW1∈𝒲⁡(Θ1)𝐄θ∼W1[D(Pθ∥PW1)],\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[-\log\frac{p_{W^{*}_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})}{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y})}\right]=\inf_{q}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[-\log\frac{q(\mathbf{Y})}{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{Y})}\right]=\sup_{W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1})}\ \mathbf{E}_{\theta\sim W_{1}}\left[D(P_{\theta}\|P_{W_{1}})\right], (22)

where the infimum is over all sub-probability densities qq over 𝐘\mathbf{Y}. (22) is just the redundancy-capacity theorem (Cover and Thomas, 1991) of information theory, and it has a data-compression interpretation. In a nutshell, for any e-variable of the form pW1​(𝐘)/p0​(𝐘)p_{W_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})/p_{0}(\mathbf{Y}), the log\log evidence log⁡pW1​(𝐘)/p0​(𝐘)\log p_{W_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})/p_{0}(\mathbf{Y}) is thought of as a difference between the code length needed to code the data using two lossless codes, one with lengths −log⁡pW1-\log p_{W_{1}}, associated with ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, and one with lengths −log⁡p0-\log p_{0}, associated with ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. (22) expresses that when choosing W1=W1∗W_{1}=W^{*}_{1}, one associates ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} with the code that minimises worst-case redundancy (the additional expected number of bits needed compared to an encoder that knows θ1∗\theta^{*}_{1}). This is in accordance with the MDL (Minimum Description Length) Principle, in which code length difference between the same two codes is used to measure evidence (Barron et al., 1998, Grünwald and Roos, 2020).

Example 5.

[Exponential Families with a point null: Jeffreys’ Prior on Θ1\Theta_{1}] To make this more concrete, let {Pθ:θ∈Θ}\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} represent a dd-dimensional exponential family given in either the mean or the canonical parameterisation. We restrict the parameter set to Θ1\Theta_{1} that is a compact subset of the interior of Θ\Theta and let Θ0\Theta_{0} be a singleton subset in the interior of Θ1\Theta_{1}. By standard properties of exponential families, the finite KL condition of Theorem 1 applies and the problem reduces to finding the prior W1∗W^{*}_{1} on Θ1\Theta_{1} that satisfies (22). (Clarke and Barron, 1994) showed that, for large nn, this prior converges in an L1L_{1}-sense to Jeffreys’ prior (‘least favourable under entropy loss’) , which is the main reason for adopting it in MDL model selection. They also showed that (22) and hence (21) is of size (d/2)​log⁡n+O⁡(1)(d/2)\log n+O(1). Thus, for point nulls and suitably truncated parameter spaces, this approach is consistent with the MDL Principle and with objective Bayes approaches based on Jeffreys prior.

Example 6.

[2×22\times 2 Tables, Continued] If Θ0\Theta_{0} is not a singleton then the simplification of (21) to (22) is not possible, and numerical simulation can be used to determine (21) and the priors appearing therein. Consider for example the 2×22\times 2 model, but now with unrestricted Θ1=(0,1)2\Theta_{1}=(0,1)^{2}. This does satisfy the regularity conditions needed for Theorem 1 to be applicable (see Appendix A.3), but it has Θ1\Theta_{1} 2-dimensional and Θ0\Theta_{0} 1-dimensional. We saw in the previous example that for 1-vs. 0-dimensional exponential family models, (21) would take on value (1/2)​log⁡n+O⁡(1)(1/2)\log n+O(1), which suggests that it is the same here, for 22- vs. 11-dimensional. This is confirmed by numerical simulations (Turner et al., 2021).

4.2 Composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, nuisance parameters present

We now consider the common situation of models that can be parameterised by Θ={(δ,γ):δ∈Δ,γ∈Γ}\Theta=\{(\delta,\gamma):\delta\in\Delta,\gamma\in\Gamma\} where δ\delta is a single parameter of interest (for simplicity taken to be a scalar) and γ\gamma represents a nuisance parameter (scalar or vector). As in Section 3.1, we want to test whether δ≥δ+\delta\geq\delta^{+} or δ≤δ−\delta\leq\delta^{-} for some δ−<δ+\delta^{-}<\delta^{+}. We thus let

Θ0={(δ,γ):δ≤δ−,γ∈Γ},vs.Θ1={(δ,γ):δ≥δ+,γ∈Γ}.\displaystyle\Theta_{0}=\{(\delta,\gamma):\delta\leq\delta^{-},\gamma\in\Gamma\},\ \ \text{vs.}\ \ \Theta_{1}=\{(\delta,\gamma):\delta\geq\delta^{+},\gamma\in\Gamma\}.\vskip 0.0pt (23)

We will first consider the simplified problem in which we test Θ0,δ−:={(δ−,γ):γ∈Γ}\Theta_{0,\delta^{-}}:=\{(\delta^{-},\gamma):\gamma\in\Gamma\} vs. Θ1,δ+:={(δ+,γ):γ∈Γ}\Theta_{1,\delta^{+}}:=\{(\delta^{+},\gamma):\gamma\in\Gamma\}, and later extend to (23). This simplified problem can be handled via a REGROW e-variable just like in the previous subsection, with now θ=(δ+,γ)\theta=(\delta^{+},\gamma): we take f⁡((δ+,γ))=GRO​((δ+,γ))f((\delta^{+},\gamma))=\text{GRO}((\delta^{+},\gamma)) and apply Theorem 1 as in (21). This gives an e-variable Eδ+∗:=pW1∗​(𝐘)/p0∗​(𝐘)E^{*}_{\delta^{+}}:=p_{W^{*}_{1}}({\bf Y})/p^{*}_{0}({\bf Y}) with W1∗W^{*}_{1} a prior on {(δ+,γ):γ∈Γ}\{(\delta^{+},\gamma):\gamma\in\Gamma\}. Using this REGROW rather than GROW approach reflects a particular interpretation of what it means for a parameter γ\gamma to be nuisance: we have no idea of what the true γ\gamma might be and are therefore prepared to incur the same expected loss of growth for not knowing γ\gamma, irrespective of what γ\gamma is. Solving this problem for all δ+≥δ−\delta^{+}\geq\delta^{-} gives us a collection of e-variables ℰ≥δ−:={Eδ∗:δ≥δ−}\mathcal{E}_{\geq\delta^{-}}:=\{E^{*}_{\delta}:\delta\geq\delta^{-}\}. Now suppose there exists another e-variable E∗E^{*} such that

supE∈ℰ≥δ−infθ∈Θ1𝐄Pθ​[log⁡E]=infθ∈Θ1𝐄Pθ​[log⁡E∗]\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}_{\geq\delta^{-}}}\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{P_{\theta}}[\log E]=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{P_{\theta}}[\log E^{*}] (24)

That is, we pick the worst-case optimal e-variable among ℰ≥δ−\mathcal{E}_{\geq\delta^{-}}, thereby applying GROW on a meta-level as it were, after restricting ourselves to e-variables that are themselves REGROW for fixed δ\delta and unknown γ\gamma. This E∗E^{*} is then our choice for solving the original problem (23).

Discussion

In our examples, we have used (and will keep using in the next section) the REGROW approach to first eliminate nuisance parameters, if they are present, followed by a GROW approach for the parameters of interest.(Turner et al., 2021, ter Schure et al., 2021) find that this gives intuitive e-variables that perform well in practical applications, not just directly in the GRO sense but also in terms of secondary measures such as a power analysis (Section 6) or as the basis of anytime-valid confidence intervals (Turner et al., 2021). Still, it may not always be the best way to go. For example, a REGROW approach for the parameter of interest when a minimum effect size is given may sometimes be sensible as well. Let us consider this a bit further for (for simplicity) the case with a minimum effect size δ+\delta^{+} but without nuisance parameters, as in Example 4. REGROW would amount here to using EW1∗=pW1​(𝐘)/pδ−​(𝐘)E^{*}_{W_{1}}=p_{W_{1}}(\mathbf{Y})/p_{\delta^{-}}(\mathbf{Y}) with some prior W1W_{1} spread out on the set Θ1={δ:δ≥δ+}\Theta_{1}=\{\delta:\delta\geq\delta^{+}\}. Then we would get 𝐄Pδ​[log⁡EW1∗]<GROW​(Θ1)​ for δ close to δ+ ;𝐄Pδ​[log⁡EW1∗]≫GROW​(Θ1)​ for δ≫δ+ \mathbf{E}_{P_{\delta}}[\log E^{*}_{W_{1}}]<\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1})\text{\ for $\delta$ close to $\delta^{+}$\ };\mathbf{E}_{P_{\delta}}[\log E^{*}_{W_{1}}]\gg\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1})\text{\ for $\delta\gg\delta^{+}$\ } so we would win if we are ‘lucky’ and it turns out that δ≫δ+\delta\gg\delta^{+}. However, in practice we often deal with small sample sizes, and δ\delta’s that may very well be very close to δ+\delta^{+}. Then (as our experiments done for the papers above indicate) the difference in ‘<<’ above is non-negligible, and the GROW approach seems safer, since for the GROW e-variable we automatically have 𝐄Pδ​[log⁡EW1∗]≥GROW​(Θ1)\mathbf{E}_{P_{\delta}}[\log E^{*}_{W_{1}}]\geq\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1}) for all δ∈Θ1\delta\in\Theta_{1}.

4.3 Theorem 1 in Full: Application to Bayesian and Sequential tt-test

If we try to apply Theorem 1 as above to the tt-test, a prototypical nuisance setting, we run into the issue that the minimum KL is not achieved. This problem can be solved by extending the theorem further, allowing for densities on a coarsening of 𝐘\mathbf{Y}. This is any random variable 𝐕\mathbf{V} that can be written as a function of 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, i.e. 𝐕=g⁡(𝐘)\mathbf{V}=g(\mathbf{Y}) for some function gg; we retrieve the previous version of Theorem 1 if we take gg the identity and 𝐕=𝐘\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{Y}. We now present Theorem 1 in full generality, allowing for such coarsening and additionally for considering the best e-variable on a modified ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, consisting of any convex set of Bayes marginal distributions with priors on Θ1\Theta_{1}. This is needed for accommodating the tt-test. It also allows us to incorporate robust Bayesian settings (Berger, 1985, Grünwald and Dawid, 2004), but we will not further pursue those here. In the theorem we use the following notation: for (sub-) distribution PP for 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, P[𝐕]P^{[\mathbf{V}]} denotes the marginal (sub-) distribution of PP for 𝐕\mathbf{V}, and p′p^{\prime} denotes its density.

Theorem 1, Full Generality Let f⁡(θ)f(\theta) be a function that is bounded on Θ1\Theta_{1}. Suppose all Pθ,Pθ′P_{\theta},P_{\theta^{\prime}} with θ,θ′∈Θ1\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta_{1} satisfy D(Pθ∥Pθ′)<∞D(P_{\theta}\|P_{\theta^{\prime}})<\infty, and have full support. Let 𝒲1⊆𝒲⁡(Θ1)\mathcal{W}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}) be convex. If for some coarsening 𝐕\mathbf{V} of 𝐘\mathbf{Y} we have:

infW1∈𝒲1infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)(D(PW1∥PW0)−f(W1))=minW1∈𝒲1infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)(D(P[𝐕]W1∥P[𝐕]W0)−f(W1))=infW0∈𝒲0​(Θ0)D(P[𝐕]W1∗∥P[𝐕]W0)−f(W∗1)<∞,\inf_{W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}\left(\ D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})-f(W_{1})\right)=\\ \min_{W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}\left(\ D(P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W_{1}}\|P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W_{0}})-f(W_{1})\right)=\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}_{0}(\Theta_{0})}D(P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W_{0}})-f(W^{*}_{1})<\infty,\vskip-10.00002pt (25)

then there exists an e-variable

Ef:=pW1∗′​(𝐕)p∗′0(𝐕),E^{f}:=\frac{p^{\prime}_{W^{*}_{1}}(\mathbf{V})}{p^{*^{\prime}}_{0}(\mathbf{V})}, (26)

The previous version of Theorem 1 is the special case obtained by setting 𝒲1=𝒲⁡(Θ1)\mathcal{W}_{1}=\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}), 𝐘=𝐕\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{V} and using linearity of expectation. We call EfE^{f} as in (27) the REGROW e-variable relative to offset ff and set of priors 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}. If ff is constant (no offset), we call it 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}-GROW, noting that it gives worst-case optimal growth rate under all priors in 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}.

The tt-test Setting

We return to the setting with a nuisance parameter with notation as in Section 4.2. Jeffreys (1961) proposed a Bayesian version of the tt-test; see also (Rouder et al., 2009). We start with the models ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} for data 𝐘=(Y1,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}) given as ℋ0={P0,σ​(𝐘)∣σ∈Γ}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0,\sigma}(\mathbf{Y})\mid\sigma\in\Gamma\}; ℋ1={Pδ,σ​(𝐘)∣(δ,σ)∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\delta,\sigma}(\mathbf{Y})\mid(\delta,\sigma)\in\Theta_{1}\}, where Δ=ℝ,Γ=ℝ+\Delta=\mathbb{R},\Gamma=\mathbb{R}^{+}, Θ1≔Δ×Γ\Theta_{1}\coloneqq\Delta\times\Gamma and Θ0={(0,σ):σ∈Γ}\Theta_{0}=\{(0,\sigma):\sigma\in\Gamma\}, and Pδ,σP_{\delta,\sigma} has density (with y¯=1n​∑i=1nyi\overline{y}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i})

pδ,σ​(y)\displaystyle p_{\delta,\sigma}(y) =1(2​π​σ2)n/2⋅exp⁡(−n2​[(y¯σ−δ)2+(1n​∑i=1n(yi−y¯)2σ2)]),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{n/2}}\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{n}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\overline{y}}{\sigma}-\delta\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\overline{y})^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right)\right]\right),

Jeffreys proposed to equip ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} with a Cauchy prior Wc​[δ]W^{\text{\sc c}}[\delta] on the effect size δ\delta, and both ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} with the scale-invariant prior measure with density wH​(σ)∝1/σw^{H}(\sigma)\propto 1/\sigma on the variance. The same formula with the same prior on σ\sigma but other priors on δ\delta was suggested by Lai (1976) with a non-Bayesian, martingale interpretation. Below we will see that, even though wH​(σ)w^{H}(\sigma) is improper (whereas the priors appearing in Theorem 1 are invariably proper), the resulting Bayes factor E∗E^{*} is an e-variable. We then present Theorem 2 which shows that, for priors W⁡[δ]W[\delta] with more than 2 moments, E∗E^{*} in fact even is 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}-GROW with 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1} the set of all product priors on δ×σ\delta\times\sigma with marginal W⁡[δ]W[\delta] on δ\delta, i.e. it has a worst-case optimal growth rate property relative to all distributions in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} compatible with W⁡[δ]W[\delta]. Thus, a form of GROW-optimality holds for most priors W⁡[δ]W[\delta] one might want to use, including standard choices (such as a standard normal) or the point prior we will suggest further below — but we do not know if it holds for the moment-less Cauchy proposed by Jeffreys.

Almost Bayesian Case: prior on δ\delta available

For any proper prior distribution W⁡[δ]W[\delta] on δ\delta and any proper prior distribution W⁡[σ]W[\sigma] on σ\sigma, we define pW⁡[δ],W⁡[σ]​(y)=∫δ∈Δ∫σ∈Γpδ,σ​(y)​d​W​[δ]​d​W​[σ],p_{W[\delta],W[\sigma]}(y)=\int_{\delta\in\Delta}\int_{\sigma\in\Gamma}p_{\delta,\sigma}(y)\,\textnormal{d}W{[\delta]}\,\textnormal{d}W{[\sigma]}, as the Bayes marginal density under the product prior W⁡[δ]×W⁡[σ]W[\delta]\times W[\sigma].

For convenience later on we set the sample space to be 𝒴n=(ℝ∖{0})×ℝn−1\mathcal{Y}^{n}=(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}, assuming beforehand that the first outcome will not be 0. Now we define 𝐕≔(V1,…,Vn)\mathbf{V}\coloneqq(V_{1},\ldots,V_{n}) with Vi=Yi/|Y1|V_{i}=Y_{i}/|Y_{1}|. We have that 𝐘\mathbf{Y} determines 𝐕\mathbf{V}, and (𝐕,Y1)(\mathbf{V},Y_{1}) determines 𝐘=(Y1,Y2,…,Yn)\mathbf{Y}=(Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots,Y_{n}). The distributions in ℋ0∪ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{0}\cup\mathcal{H}_{1} can thus alternatively be thought of as distributions on the pair (𝐕,Y1)(\mathbf{V},Y_{1}). 𝐕\mathbf{V} is “𝐘\mathbf{Y} with the scale divided out”: as is well-known (Lai, 1976, Berger et al., 1998) and easily shown (Appendix B.3), under all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, i.e. all P0,σP_{0,\sigma} with σ>0\sigma>0, 𝐕\mathbf{V} has the same distribution P0​[𝐕]P_{0}[\mathbf{V}] with density p0′p^{\prime}_{0}. In the same way, one shows that under all PW⁡[δ],σ{P}_{W[\delta],\sigma} with σ>0\sigma>0, 𝐕\mathbf{V} has the same pdf pW⁡[δ]′p^{\prime}_{W[\delta]} (which therefore does not depend on the prior on σ\sigma). We now get that, with

E∗≔pW⁡[δ]′​(𝐕)p0′​(𝐕),E^{*}\coloneqq\frac{p^{\prime}_{W[\delta]}(\mathbf{V})}{p^{\prime}_{0}(\mathbf{V})}, (28)

we must have 𝐄𝐕∼P​[E∗]=1\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{V}\sim P}[E^{*}]=1 for all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, hence it is an e variable. Remarkably, this ‘scale-free’ e-variable coincides with the Bayes factor one gets if one uses, for σ\sigma, the prior wH​(σ)=1/σw^{H}(\sigma)=1/\sigma suggested by Jeffreys, and treats σ\sigma and δ\delta as independent. That is (Lai, 1976, page 273) (a full derivation is in Appendix B.3), we have

∫σpW⁡[δ],σ​(𝐘)​wH​(σ)​d​σ∫σp0,σ​(𝐘)​wH​(σ)​d​σ=pW⁡[δ]′​(𝐕)p0′​(𝐕)=E∗.\frac{\int_{\sigma}p_{W[\delta],\sigma}(\mathbf{Y})w^{H}(\sigma)\,\textnormal{d}\sigma}{\int_{\sigma}{p}_{0,\sigma}(\mathbf{Y})w^{H}(\sigma)\,\textnormal{d}\sigma}=\frac{p^{\prime}_{W[\delta]}(\mathbf{V})}{p^{\prime}_{0}(\mathbf{V})}=E^{*}. (29)

Despite its improperness, wHw^{H} induces a valid e-variable when used in the Bayes factor. The equivalence of this Bayes factor to E∗E^{*} simply means that it manages to ignore the ‘nuisance’ part of the model and models the likelihood of the scale-free 𝐕\mathbf{V} instead. The reason this is possible is that wHw^{H} coincides with the right-Haar prior for this problem (Eaton, 1989, Berger et al., 1998), about which we will say more below. Amazingly, it turns out that the e-variable (29) has a GROW property (among all e-variables for data 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, not just the coarsened 𝐕\mathbf{V}) under the weak condition that the prior W⁡[δ]W[\delta] has a (2+ϵ)(2+\epsilon)th moment.
