REGROW-GROW safe tt-test with minimum effect sizes

Suppose we want to test Θ1\Theta_{1} vs. Θ0\Theta_{0} as in (23) with fixed effect sizes δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-} and with σ2\sigma^{2} in the role of γ\gamma. We proceed exactly as we did underneath (23): we first consider the test {(δ+,σ2):σ2>0}\{(\delta^{+},\sigma^{2}):\sigma^{2}>0\} vs. {(δ−,σ2):σ2>0}\{(\delta^{-},\sigma^{2}):\sigma^{2}>0\} for the fixed given δ+\delta^{+} using the REGROW criterion with f⁡((δ,σ))=GRO​(δ,σ)f((\delta,\sigma))=\text{GRO}(\delta,\sigma). We have (Koolen and Grünwald, 2021, Section 4.3) that f⁡(δ+,σ)=(n/2)​log⁡(1+δ+2)f(\delta^{+},\sigma)=(n/2)\log(1+\delta^{+2}) is constant on σ\sigma. Therefore we can use Theorem 1 in its most general form above in combination with Theorem 2 (applied with point prior W⁡[δ]W[\delta] on δ+\delta^{+}) to conclude that (both the GROW and) the REGROW e-variable are given by Eδ+∗:=pδ+′​(𝐕)/pδ−′​(𝐕)E^{*}_{\delta^{+}}:=p^{\prime}_{\delta^{+}}(\mathbf{V})/p^{\prime}_{\delta^{-}}(\mathbf{V}). Since Proposition 3 is applicable to sets of distributions defined on 𝐕\mathbf{V} rather than 𝐘\mathbf{Y} (details in Appendix B.3), we find that, with ℰ≥δ+:={Eδ∗:δ≥δ−}\mathcal{E}_{\geq\delta^{+}}:=\{E^{*}_{\delta}:\delta\geq\delta^{-}\} that supE∈ℰ≥δ+infσ>0,δ≥δ+𝐄𝐘∼Pδ,σ​[log⁡E]=infσ>0,δ≥δ+𝐄𝐘∼Pδ,σ​[log⁡Eδ+∗]\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}_{\geq\delta^{+}}}\inf_{\sigma>0,\delta\geq\delta^{+}}\mathbf{E}_{{\bf Y}\sim P_{\delta,\sigma}}[\log E]=\inf_{\sigma>0,\delta\geq\delta^{+}}\mathbf{E}_{{\bf Y}\sim P_{\delta,\sigma}}[\log E^{*}_{\delta^{+}}] so Eδ+∗E^{*}_{\delta^{+}} may be thought of as first applying REGROW, to get rid of the nuisance parameter, and then applying GROW — just like in the 2×22\times 2 Example 7.

Extension to General Group Invariant Bayes Factors

In a series of papers (Berger et al., 1998, Dass and Berger, 2003, Bayarri et al., 2012), Berger and collaborators developed a theory of Bayes factors for ℋ0={P0,γ:γ∈Γ}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0,\gamma}:\gamma\in\Gamma\} and ℋ1={Pδ,γ:δ∈Δ,γ∈Γ}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\delta,\gamma}:\delta\in\Delta,\gamma\in\Gamma\} with a nuisance parameter (vector) γ\gamma that appears in both models and that satisfies a group invariance; the Bayesian tt-test is the special case with γ=σ,Γ=ℝ+\gamma=\sigma,\Gamma=\mathbb{R}^{+} and with the scalar multiplication group and δ\delta an ‘effect size’. Other examples include regression based on mixtures of gg-priors (Liang et al., 2008), testing a Weibull vs. the log-normal and many more (Dass and Berger, 2003). The reasoning of the first part of this section straightforwardly generalises to all such cases: the Bayes factor based on using the right Haar measure on γ\gamma in both models gives rise to an e-variable. Theorem 4.2. of Perez et al. (2022) shows that, if the underlying group satisfies a condition called amenability (which holds, e.g., for scaling as in the t-test, but also for e.g. rotations and affine transformations as in parametric linear regression models), then the resulting Bayes factor is GROW relative to a suitably defined set 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}. Theorem 2 above is the very special case of their result when instantiated with γ\gamma instantiated to the variance in the t-test (scaling). Although its proof is quite different, the general result may be viewed as the ‘e-variant’ of the classical Hunt-Stein theorem (Lehmann et al., 2005, Section 8.5), with ‘power’ in that theorem replaced by ‘GROW’. (Perez et al., 2022, Proposition 4.4) then implies that in all such cases, this GROW Bayes factor is in fact also REGROW. Remarkably therefore, with parameters representing group transformations, unlike e.g. for the 2×22\times 2 case, GROW and REGROW e-variables generally coincide.

5 (RE)GRO(W), Optional Continuation and Stopping

We now address two related questions:

  1. 1.

    We focused on Type-I error safety under optional continuation (OC). Can we also get safety under optional stopping (OS), and what is the difference?

  2. 2.

    The GRO-criteria were chosen to optimise expected capital (logarithmic) growth ‘locally’, within a study. How well do GRO-criteria go together with OC over several studies?

To make the questions concrete, we consider a specific set-up with data stream Yj,1,Yj,2,…Y_{j,1},Y_{j,2},\ldots corresponding to the jj-th study to be performed. In the first study we observe batch of outcomes 𝐘(1)=(Y1,1,…,Y1,N(1))\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}=(Y_{1,1},\ldots,Y_{1,N_{(1)}}); in the second study (if it is performed at all) 𝐘(2)=(Y2,1,…,Y2,N(2))\mathbf{Y}_{(2)}=(Y_{2,1},\ldots,Y_{2,N_{(2)}}); and so on. For further simplicity we will assume that all Yj,iY_{j,i} are i.i.d. The set-up slightly differs from Example 3 in which the second study’s data was part of the same stream as the first; at the expense of additional notation, everything that follows can be formalized in that setting as well.

The conditional e-variables determining our test martingale are now determined by a sequence of stopping times N(1),N(2),…N_{(1)},N_{(2)},\ldots. The first stopping time N(1)N_{(1)} is defined as a stopping time on the first sequence Y1,1,Y1,2,…Y_{1,1},Y_{1,2},\ldots relative to filtration (σ⁡(Y1n))n(\sigma(Y_{1}^{n}))_{n} and defines a stopped σ\sigma-algebra ℱ(1):=σ⁡(Y1N(1))=σ⁡(𝐘(1))\mathcal{F}_{(1)}:=\sigma(Y_{1}^{N_{(1)}})=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}). N(2)N_{(2)} is defined on the second sequence Y2,1,Y2,2,…Y_{2,1},Y_{2,2},\ldots, but it is also allowed to depend on previous data 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}, i.e it is a stopping time relative to filtration (σ⁡(𝐘(1),Y2n))n(\sigma({\bf Y}_{(1)},Y_{2}^{n}))_{n}, and defines a stopped σ\sigma-algebra ℱ(2):=σ⁡(𝐘(1),𝐘(2))\mathcal{F}_{(2)}:=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\mathbf{Y}_{(2)}). In general, N(m)N_{(m)} is defined relative to filtration σ​(𝐘(1),…,𝐘(m−1),Ymn)n\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m-1)},Y_{m}^{n})_{n}, and defines a stopped σ\sigma-algebra ℱ(m):=σ⁡(𝐘(1),…,𝐘(m))\mathcal{F}_{(m)}:=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m)}). We let 𝒩(m)\mathcal{N}_{(m)} be the collection of all stopping times for the mm-th study, i.e. relative to σ​(𝐘(1),…,𝐘(m−1),Ym,1,…,Ym,n)n\sigma(\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(m-1)},Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n})_{n}. The sequence of stopped σ\sigma-algebras thus defines a new filtration (ℱ(m))m(\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m}, which we call the filtration at the study level, since ℱ(m)\mathcal{F}_{(m)} denotes all information available after mm studies or trials have been completed — it is the filtration referred to in Proposition 2 (for the t-test we need to extend this set-up a little, see Example 8).

OC vs. OS

In the optional continuation setting, we assume that, after having observed and analyzed m−1m-1 studies, we either stop, or continue to the next study. In the latter case we need to specify a stopping time N(m)∈𝒩(m)N_{(m)}\in\mathcal{N}_{(m)} and a conditional e-variable E(m)∈ℰ(m)E_{(m)}\in\mathcal{E}_{(m)} where ℰ(m)\mathcal{E}_{(m)} is the set of all ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-conditional e-variables. For example, in the setting of Example 1, with a simple null ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} and composite alternative ℋ1={Pθ:θ∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_{1}\} and N(m)∈𝒩(m)N_{(m)}\in\mathcal{N}_{(m)} an arbitrary stopping time for the mm-th study, eN(m),W​(Ym,1,…,Ym,N(m)):=pW​(Ym,1,…,Ym,N(m))/p0​(Ym,1,…,Ym,N(m))e_{N_{(m)},W}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,N_{(m)}}):=p_{W}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,N_{(m)}})/p_{0}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,N_{(m)}}) is an e-variable for every ‘prior’ distribution WW on Θ1\Theta_{1} (here we generalize the notation of Example 1 to allow for data-dependent stopping times). In this setting the analyst can freely choose (or somebody else can impose) any N(m)N_{(m)} and any WW and use the corresponding e-variable eN(m),We_{N_{(m)},W}; all such e-variables are contained in the set ℰ(m)\mathcal{E}_{(m)}. As explained in Example 1, this includes the choice to set W(m):=W(1)W_{(m)}:=W_{(1)} (re-use the original prior) and the choice to set W(m):=W(1)(⋅∣𝐘(m−1))W_{(m)}:=W_{(1)}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}), i.e. use the Bayes posterior based on the previous studies.

We can now interpret our various GRO criteria as each providing a prescription to choose specific elements of ℰN(m)\mathcal{E}_{N_{(m)}}, for all stopping times N(m)N_{(m)} that are constant given the outcomes of previous studies 𝐘(m−1)\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}, i.e. that are ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-measurable. To see this, note that each GRO criterion in combination with ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} defines, for each nn, an e-variable S[n]S^{[n]} for a single sequence Y1,…,YnY_{1},\ldots,Y_{n}. In all cases, this can be written as S[n]=s[n]​(Yn)S^{[n]}=s^{[n]}(Y^{n}) for some function s[n]s^{[n]}; the function s[n]s^{[n]} is what is really specified; we call s[1],s[2],…s^{[1]},s^{[2]},\ldots an e-specification. If N(m):=nmN_{(m)}:=n_{m}, we can thus simply set E(m):=s[nm]​(Ym,1,…,Ym,nm)E_{(m)}:=s^{[n_{m}]}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n_{m}}). We call this the plug-in method for constructing E(m)E_{(m)} from specification s[1],s[2],…s^{[1]},s^{[2]},\ldots (such specification may correspond to one of our GRO criteria, but in general it could be arrived at in different ways as well) . The running product of E(m)E_{(m)} thus constructed provides, via Proposition 2, a test martingale at the study level.

In contrast, optional stopping scenarios usually concern only a single data-level process Y1,Y2,…Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots, without any super-structure in terms of subsequent studies. The scenario is completely determined by a sequence of conditional e-variables S1,S2,…S_{1},S_{2},\ldots, i.e., applying Definition 1 at the data level, such that for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, for all P∈ℋ0:𝐄P[Sn∣ℱn−1]≤1 a.s.\text{for all $P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}$:}\ \ {\bf E}_{P}[S_{n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\leq 1\text{\ a.s.}, with ℱn=σ⁡(Yn)\mathcal{F}_{n}=\sigma(Y^{n}). Their running product S[1],S[2],…S^{[1]},S^{[2]},\ldots (with S[n]=∏i=1nSiS^{[n]}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}) then forms a test martingale. Recall from Corollary 1 in Section 1.3 that for any nonnegative random process E(1),E(2),…E^{(1)},E^{(2)},\ldots at the study level (adapted to (ℱ(m))m(\mathcal{F}_{(m)})_{m}) we say that the corresponding threshold test is safe under OC (with respect to Type-I error) if the Ville-Robbins inequality (7) holds. Extending this definition in the natural way, we say, for a data-level process of nonnegative random variables S[1],S[2],…S^{[1]},S^{[2]},\ldots, i.e. with S[j]S^{[j]} adapted to ℱj\mathcal{F}_{j}, that the corresponding threshold test is safe under OS (with respect to Type-I error) if again the Ville-Robbins inequality holds (with E(n):=S[n]E^{(n)}:=S^{[n]}).

Sequentially Decomposable e-Specifications

In many (not all) cases, the GRO-specification s[1],s[2],…s^{[1]},s^{[2]},\ldots forms itself a test martingale relative to some filtration (𝒢n)n(\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n}: there exist a sequence of functions s1,s2,…s_{1},s_{2},\ldots, with sis_{i} a function on 𝒴i\mathcal{Y}^{i}, such that, for all nn, s[n]​(Yn)=∏i=1nSis^{[n]}(Y^{n})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}S_{i} with Si:=si​(Yi)S_{i}:=s_{i}(Y^{i}) and {Si}i\{S_{i}\}_{i} is a conditional e-variable collection relative to filtration (𝒢n)n(\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n}. We will say that such an e-variable specification is sequentially decomposable, or seqdec for short, relative to filtration (𝒢n)n(\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n}; in all our examples except the t-test (Example 8) we can take 𝒢n=σ⁡(Yn)\mathcal{G}_{n}=\sigma(Y^{n}). Seqdec specifications have a direct link with the OS setting, resulting in three remarkable properties: first, assuming still that data are i.i.d., any study-level test martingale process we can construct via the plug-in method (see above) based on a seqdec specification also defines a sequence of conditional e-variables and hence a test martingale at the corresponding concatenated data level Y1′,Y2′,…Y^{\prime}_{1},Y^{\prime}_{2},\ldots where Yi′Y^{\prime}_{i} is arrived at by relabeling Y1,1,Y1,2,…,Y1,N(1),Y2,1,Y2,2,…,Y2,N(2),Y3,1,…Y_{1,1},Y_{1,2},\ldots,Y_{1,N_{(1)}},Y_{2,1},Y_{2,2},\ldots,Y_{2,N_{(2)}},Y_{3,1},\ldots in order (so that e.g. YN(1)+N(2)′=Y2,N(2)Y^{\prime}_{N_{(1)}+N_{(2)}}=Y_{2,N_{(2)}}). This defines a concatenated data-level filtration (𝒢t′)t(\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t})_{t} with 𝒢t′=σ⁡(Y1′,…,Yt′)\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{t}=\sigma(Y^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,Y^{\prime}_{t}). The corresponding sequence of conditional e-variables is then given by S1′,S2′,…S^{\prime}_{1},S^{\prime}_{2},\ldots where, for T(0):=0T_{(0)}:=0, m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤i<N(m)1\leq i<N_{(m)}, T(m):=∑j=1mN(j)T_{(m)}:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}N_{(j)}, we set ST(m)+i′:=si​(Ym,1,…,Ym,i)S^{\prime}_{T_{(m)}+i}:=s_{i}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i}). This means that besides engaging in optional continuation, we can also safely do optional stopping at this concatenated-data level, since the Ville-Robbins inequality holds at this level by Corollary 1.

Second, we can use seqdec specifications to extend the plug-in method (which required constant stopping times N(m)N_{(m)}) to prescribe conditional E-variables for stopping times N(m)N_{(m)} that are not constant given 𝐘(m−1)\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}: for arbitrary N(m)∈𝒩(m)N_{(m)}\in\mathcal{N}_{(m)}, we set E(m):=∏i=1N(m)si​(Ym,1,…,Ym,i)E_{(m)}:=\prod_{i=1}^{N_{(m)}}s_{i}(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i}). By construction, this reduces to the plug-in method whenever N(m)N_{(m)} is constant given 𝐘(m−1)\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}, so it is a proper extension, and it follows as a direct corollary of the fact that E(m)E_{(m)} can be rewritten as ∏i=1N(m)ST(m−1)+i′\prod_{i=1}^{N_{(m)}}S^{\prime}_{T_{(m-1)}+i}, i.e. a product of factors in a test martingale, that any E(m)E_{(m)} constructed in this manner for any seqdec specification is a ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-conditional e-variable.

Third, seqdec specifications allow for alternative ways to create study-level processes from e-specifications beyond the plug-in method used thus far. For example, we can set E(m):=∏i=1N(m)sT(m−1)+i​(𝐘(m−1),Ym,1,…,Ym,i)E_{(m)}:=\prod_{i=1}^{N_{(m)}}s_{T_{(m-1)}+i}(\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)},Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,i}) for arbitrary stopping times N(1),…,N(m)N_{(1)},\ldots,N_{(m)}. Once again, this also defines a martingale at the concatenated data-level — it is simply the martingale that arises if we view the mm studies as one single, long sequence of T(m)T_{(m)} data points. We call this the sequential application of the e-variable specification — see Figure 3.

Example 8.

All GRO-type specifications based on a simple ℋ0={P0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{0}\} are likelihood ratios s[i]=q⁡(Yi)/p0​(Yi)s^{[i]}=q(Y^{i})/p_{0}(Y^{i}), and hence will be seqdec and can thus be combined with optional stopping. In Example 1, choosing W(m):=W(1)|𝐘(m−1)W_{(m)}:=W_{(1)}\mid\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)} to be the Bayesian posterior corresponds to the sequential application of the W(1)W_{(1)}-GRO specification of Section 2.2; using W(m):=W(1)W_{(m)}:=W_{(1)} corresponds to the plug-in application of the W(1)W_{(1)}-GRO application. This illustrates that we may think of our GRO criteria not as prescribing a single choice E(m)∈ℰN(m)E_{(m)}\in\mathcal{E}_{N_{(m)}}, but rather as suggesting to choose E(m)E_{(m)} from a preferred subset ℰN(m)′\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{N_{(m)}} of ℰN(m)\mathcal{E}_{N_{(m)}}; the end-user may then pick any e-variable in ℰN(m)′\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{N_{(m)}}. For example, in the case of Example 1 with simple ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, we may further specify a set of distributions 𝒲1|𝐘(m−1)\mathcal{W}_{1}\mid\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)} on Θ1\Theta_{1} that we deem ‘reasonable’ given previous outcomes 𝐘(m−1)\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}, which may include the full Bayesian posterior, the originally used prior, combinations of these, tempered posteriors and so on; and we may then suggest the set ℰN(m)′\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{N_{(m)}} of all e-variables for the mm-th study based on a prior in 𝒲1|𝐘(m−1)\mathcal{W}_{1}\mid\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}.

For the (RE)GRO(W)-specifications with composite null, one immediately verifies that those of Proposition 3 and Example 4 also are seqdec, since they equal the likelihood ratio between the same two distributions Pδ+P_{\delta^{+}} and Pδ−P_{\delta^{-}} irrespective of nn. The t-test GROW/REGROW e-variables for arbitrary prior W⁡[δ]W[\delta] on δ\delta as in (28) are seqdec as well, but to formalize this statement we have to extend the setting. In general, the seqdec definition makes sense for every filtration (𝒢n)n(\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n} with 𝒢n=σ⁡(Vn)\mathcal{G}_{n}=\sigma(V^{n}) where Vn=vn​(Yn)V_{n}=v_{n}(Y^{n}) for some sequence of functions v1,v2,…v_{1},v_{2},\ldots defined on 𝒴1,𝒴2,…\mathcal{Y}^{1},\mathcal{Y}^{2},\ldots respectively. The previous definition is the special case with vn​(Yn)=Ynv_{n}(Y^{n})=Y_{n}. In the t-test example we can take VnV_{n} as in Section 4.3 such that vn​(Y1,…,Yn)=Yn/|Y1|v_{n}(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n})=Y_{n}/|Y_{1}|. Let us illustrate how, with this coarser filtration, we can still apply the plug-in method for non-constant stopping times N(m)N_{(m)}. For this, we also have to coarsen the filtrations relative to which the N(m)N_{(m)} are defined : the set of allowed stopping times 𝒩(m)\mathcal{N}_{(m)} is now restricted to lie in (ℱ(m−1)∪σ⁡(Vm,1,…,Vm,n))n(\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}\cup\sigma(V_{m,1},\ldots,V_{m,n}))_{n} with Vj,n=vj,n​(Yj,1,…,Yj,n)V_{j,n}=v_{j,n}(Y_{j,1},\ldots,Y_{j,n}) for some collection of functions (vj,n)n(v_{j,n})_{n} (recall that before they were members of (ℱ(m−1)∪σ⁡(Ym,1,…,Ym,n))n(\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}\cup\sigma(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n}))_{n}) . For the tt-test example we set vj,n​(Yj,1,…,Yj,n)=Yj,n/|Yj,1|v_{j,n}(Y_{j,1},\ldots,Y_{j,n})=Y_{j,n}/|Y_{j,1}|. The study-level filtrations ℱ(1):=σ(Y(1)),ℱ(2):=σ(Y(1),Y(2)),…\mathcal{F}_{(1)}:=\sigma(Y_{(1)}),\mathcal{F}_{(2)}:=\sigma(Y_{(1)},Y_{(2)}),\ldots remain unchanged and do not hide any information in the Y(j)Y_{(j)}. In practice the restriction of 𝒩(m)\mathcal{N}_{(m)} will not be of much concern since ‘most’ stopping times are still allowed, including the most aggressive stopping rule: stop the mm-th study at the smallest n′n^{\prime} such that ∏i=1n′si​(Vm,i)≥1/α(m)\prod_{i=1}^{n^{\prime}}s_{i}(V_{m,i})\geq 1/\alpha_{(m)}, where α(m−1)\alpha_{(m-1)} is some threshold that is allowed to depend on 𝐘(m−1)\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)}. We can also allow for the sequential (rather than plug-in) application of the t-test e-variable specification so that effectively we view all studies as subsequent outcomes of a single study, by restricting the filtrations in a slightly different way; we omit the details. We can even let the choice between a sequential or plug-in choice for E(m)E_{(m)} depend on past data, but this requires further generalizations of the ℱm\mathcal{F}_{m} and (vj,n)n(v_{j,n})_{n} definitions that we shall not pursue here.

Summarizing, the practical setting we have in mind when we speak about OS and OC respectively is quite different: OC concerns study-level martingales constructed by deciding, on the fly , after the m−1m-1-st study, whether to continue to the mm-th study and if so, what new ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}-conditional e-variable to take from the set ℰ(m)\mathcal{E}_{(m)} of possible e-variables of use. OS is about data-level martingales with only a stop/continue choice. Nevertheless, the formal definitions of (Type-I error) ‘safety under OS’ and ‘safety under OC’ only differ in that ‘study-level’ is replaced by ‘data-level’. We may say that combining e-variables E(m)E_{(m)} by multiplication is always Type-I error safe under OC. If the e-variable prescription used to construct E(m)E_{(m)} has the seqdec property, then the stopping times N(m)N_{(m)} used in each study do not need to be specified before the study starts and can even be externally imposed, so that we have Type-I error safety not just under OC but also under OS within each individual study.

There is one final subtlety to consider: in the OS setting, with a single stream of data Y1,Y2,…Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots and conditional e-variables S1,S2,…S_{1},S_{2},\ldots and test martingale S[1],S[2],…S^{[1]},S^{[2]},\ldots, the Ville-Robbins inequality (7) implies that our Type-I error bound α\alpha is guaranteed no matter when we stop — in particular, the actual stopping time does not have to be taken relative to the filtration (𝒢n)n(\mathcal{G}_{n})_{n} — we may even peek into the future to decide whether to stop now. This suggests that our care in specifying the correct filtrations for the t-test was unnecessary — it seems we can use any stopping rule we like! But this becomes incorrect once we move from OS at the data-level to OC at the study-level: if, in the t-test setting with the plug-in construction of the e-variable E(m)E_{(m)} for the mm-th study, we were to set the N(m)N_{(m)} so that they are not stopping times relative to (ℱ(m−1)∪σ⁡(Vm,1,…,Vm,n))n(\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}\cup\sigma(V_{m,1},\ldots,V_{m,n}))_{n} but only relative to the more refined (ℱ(m−1)∪σ⁡(Ym,1,…,Ym,n))n(\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}\cup\sigma(Y_{m,1},\ldots,Y_{m,n}))_{n} , we could end up creating fake conditional e-variables at the study-level, i.e. so that 𝐄P0​[E(m)∣ℱ(m−1)]>1\mathbf{E}_{P_{0}}[E_{(m)}\mid\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)}]>1 for all mm ((Perez et al., 2022, Appendix B) constructs such a random variable for the t-test). And then the Ville-Robbins inequality may not hold any more at the study-level, and we loose the Type-I error guarantee under optional continuation.

Local vs. Global GRO

Now consider two data streams, Y1,1,…,Y1,n1Y_{1,1},\ldots,Y_{1,n_{1}} and Y2,1,…,Y2,n2Y_{2,1},\ldots,Y_{2,n_{2}} of fixed lengths n1n_{1} and n2n_{2}. We may alternatively model these two streams as a single stream Y1′,…,Yn1+n2′Y^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,Y^{\prime}_{n_{1}+n_{2}} of length n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2}. If we use an e-variable specification with the seqdec property to generate a study-level test martingale in the sequential way (i.e. not the plug-in way) described above, we will get that, E(2)=E(1)⋅E(2)E^{(2)}=E_{(1)}\cdot E_{(2)} constructed for the first two data streams (with E(1)=∏i=1n1si​(Yi)E_{(1)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{1}}s_{i}(Y^{i}) and E(2)=∏i=1n2sn1+i​(Y′n1+i)E_{(2)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{2}}s_{n_{1}+i}(Y^{\prime n_{1}+i})) coincides with E(1)′=∏i=1n1+n2s[i]​(Yi′)E^{\prime}_{(1)}=\prod_{i=1}^{n_{1}+n_{2}}s^{[i]}(Y^{\prime}_{i}) constructed for the single alternative stream. We may thus say that the sequential application of seqdec e-specifications is always coherent: applying the specification sequentially-‘locally’ (separately for both studies) or sequentially-globally (for the concatenated data viewed as one study) gives the same result. For example, the Bayesian WW-GRO specification of Section 2.2, the GROW specification of Proposition 3 and Example 4 and the GROW and REGROW specifications in the t-test example are all seqdec and hence all have this coherence property when applied sequentially. Sometimes the sequential application of an E-prescription is not feasible or desirable; for example, not all details of previous data may be known. We may then prefer the plug-in application of the E-prescription. Unfortunately, the seqdec property is not sufficient to get coherence for the plug-in method: clearly, if we use the same prior W(1)W_{(1)} as prior in the Bayesian Example 3 for the first and the second study, this leads to different E(2)E^{(2)} and E(1)′E^{\prime}_{(1)}, the latter being equivalent to using the posterior of the first study as prior in the second. A sufficient condition for a plug-in application to satisfy coherence after all is that it satisfies both the seqdec property, and further that sis_{i}, with Si=si​(Yi)S_{i}=s_{i}(Y^{i}) as in the definition of seqdec, can be rewritten as si​(Yi)=s′​(Yi)s_{i}(Y^{i})=s^{\prime}(Y_{i}) for a single function s′s^{\prime}, for all ii. Then in fact the plug-in and the sequential application of the e-prescription will coincide, and coherence is guaranteed. This happens in the subset of our examples in which s[i]​(Yi)s^{[i]}(Y^{i}) takes the form q⁡(Yi)/p⁡(Yi)q(Y^{i})/p(Y^{i}) for the same pp and qq, for all ii, as happens e.g. in Example 4.

An Open Question concerning GRO

In practice we may very well be in a situation in which OS at the data-level is desirable (see the next section for why it would be), so we want to use a seqdec specification, yet the GRO criterion we are interested in does not give one — Example 9 illustrates this for the 2×22\times 2 case. We may then try the following approach, which for simplicity we only describe for the REGROW criterion: let EnfE^{f}_{n} be the REGROW e-variable (19) achieving (20) with f​(θ)=GRO​(θ)f(\theta)=\text{GRO}(\theta) for samples of size nn. We try to find a sequence of e-variables E1,E2,…E_{1},E_{2},\ldots such that EiE_{i} is a σ⁡(Yi−1)\sigma(Y^{i-1})-conditional e-variable for YiY_{i} and the product e-variable E[n]:=∏i=1nEiE^{[n]}:=\prod_{i=1}^{n}E_{i} achieves (20) to within some fixed ϵ\epsilon for all nn larger than some minimal n0n_{0}, i.e.

infθ∈Θ1(𝐄𝐘∼Pθ​[log⁡E[n]]−GRO​(θ))≥infθ∈Θ1(𝐄𝐘∼Pθ​[log⁡Enf]−GRO​(θ))−ϵ.\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log E^{[n]}]-\text{GRO}(\theta)\ )\geq\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{\theta}}[\log E^{f}_{n}]-\text{GRO}(\theta)\ )-\epsilon. (31)

By construction, the sequence E[1],E[2],…E^{[1]},E^{[2]},\ldots is seqdec and allows for optional stopping, and if we can find E1,E2,…E_{1},E_{2},\ldots such that ϵ\epsilon is small for all nn larger than or equal to the n0n_{0} corresponding to the smallest sample we’d ever be interested in analyzing, we can say that the full process (and not just an instance at a fixed nn) is ‘almost’ REGROW in the desired sense.

Example 9.

Turner et al. (2021) successfully use this idea for the 2×22\times 2 model. We illustrate this confining ourselves for simplicity to a stream of paired data, i.e. X1=a,X2=b,X3=a,X4=b,…X_{1}=a,X_{2}=b,X_{3}=a,X_{4}=b,\ldots. First, we note that directly applying the idea above will not work. To see this, consider the simple alternative Θ1={(μ1|a,μ1|b)}\Theta_{1}=\{(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})\}. According to the composite null, the YiY_{i} are i.i.d. Bernoulli with parameter μ∈[0,1]\mu\in[0,1], but the GROW​(Θ1)=GRO​((μ1|a,μ1|b))\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1})=\text{GRO}((\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}))- e-variable for such a ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and single data point YiY_{i} is the trivial E≡1E\equiv 1. Thus we would get all EiE_{i} equal to 11, and zero growth. However, if we analyze the data in batches of size 22, so set Y1′=(Y1,Y2),Y2′=(Y3,Y4)Y^{\prime}_{1}=(Y_{1},Y_{2}),Y^{\prime}_{2}=(Y_{3},Y_{4}) and take as Ei′=e⁡(Yi′)E^{\prime}_{i}={\rm e}(Y^{\prime}_{i}) the (nontrivial) (μ1|a,μ1|b)(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})-GRO-e-variable for Yi′=(Y2​i−1,Y2​i)Y^{\prime}_{i}=(Y_{2i-1},Y_{2i}) then E′[n]=∏i=1nEi′E^{\prime[n]}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}E^{\prime}_{i} is the (μ1|a,μ1|b)(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})-GRO-e-variable for all nn: we have the seqdec property and coherence, both for the sequential and for the plug-in method of applying the (μ1|a,μ1|b)(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})-GRO-prescription. Now in practice we want to consider a composite alternative — say we consider the full alternative Θ1=[0,1]2\Theta_{1}=[0,1]^{2}. Then the REGROW prescription will not be seqdec - the prior W1∗W^{*}_{1} in (19) depends on the sample size nn. However it turns out that for a particular choice of prior WW (Turner et al. (2021) find it to be the beta-prior with parameters α=β=0.18\alpha=\beta=0.18) we have the following: if, for all ii, we take Ei′E^{\prime}_{i} the W|Y′i−1W\mid Y^{\prime i-1}-GRO e-variable, W|Y′i−1W\mid Y^{\prime i-1} being the posterior based on Y′i−1Y^{\prime i-1}, then we numerically find that E′[n]=∏i=1nEi′E^{\prime[n]}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}E^{\prime}_{i} is, for all but the smallest nn, very close to the REGROW e-variable EnfE^{f}_{n} for that nn, i.e. it achieves (31) for small ϵ\epsilon.

The example raises an important question: under what conditions (on model, minimal batch sizes and the like) can we create a seqdec specification that behaves optimally for our desired GRO criterion (as in Section 2.2 with WW-GRO, and in Example 4, with the GROW criterion) or almost optimally (as in the 2×22\times 2 example above with batch size 2, with the REGROW criterion)?

6 Competitiveness: GRO and Power

What sample size should we minimally plan for in a study so that we may expect a useful result? The answer depends on whether one looks at e-values purely as measures of evidence, without an accept/reject decision attached, or whether one considers such decisions after all. In the latter case, we can ask, more generally, how competitive e-value based tests are, in terms of required sample size, compared to the standard fixed-sample size Neyman-Pearson approach. We consider the cases without and with accept/reject decisions in turn.

e-Values as Evidence

e-values may be viewed simply as a measure of evidence, extending the evidential interpretation of likelihood ratios (Royall, 2000). They are then certainly competitive in every sense: for simple ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} they coincide with likelihood ratios and Bayes factors, and will give thus as much evidence as these notions do; for composite ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, GRO(W) e-variables are designed to give as much expected log-evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} as possible without violating the optional continuation requirement — in practice in some cases giving a bit more, and in some cases a bit less evidence against the null than standard Bayes factors (see Turner et al. (2021) for a practical example).

Now suppose we have a minimal effect size δ\delta in mind, and we plan a study in which obtaining data is expensive. What sample size should we plan for? One option is to pick a certain target growth LL (essentially the logarithm of Shafer (2021)’s notion of “implied target”) and determine the sample size at which we expect to gain LL. To illustrate, consider the 1-dimensional exponential family case of Example 4 with Θ0={0}\Theta_{0}=\{0\}. We know that, for a sample of size nn , under all θ1∈Θ1\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1} with Θ1={θ1:θ1≥δ}\Theta_{1}=\{\theta_{1}:\theta_{1}\geq\delta\}, we have GROW(Θ1)=nD(Pδ∥P0)\text{GROW}(\Theta_{1})=nD(P_{\delta}\|P_{0}) where D(Pδ∥P0)D(P_{\delta}\|P_{0}) is the KL divergence for 1 outcome. We then calculate nGROWn_{\text{GROW}} as the smallest nn such that nD(Pδ∥P0)≥LnD(P_{\delta}\|P_{0})\geq L, i.e. nGROW=⌈L/D(Pδ∥P0)⌉n_{\text{GROW}}=\lceil L/D(P_{\delta}\|P_{0})\rceil. In the Gaussian location model, D(Pδ∥P0)=δ2/2D(P_{\delta}\|P_{0})=\delta^{2}/2, so n=⌈2​L/δ2⌉n=\lceil 2L/\delta^{2}\rceil. We return to the question of choosing LL below.

e-Values for Decisions

We can also use e-values in the traditional setting, in which a study ends with an accept/reject decision — with the proviso that any decision is provisional, since there always is an option to continue and combine the results with a new study. For better or worse, this is the paradigm that researchers often have to work in, and within this paradigm they will inevitably be interested in the power for the experiment ahead. They will then plan for a certain sample size nn to achieve such power, with a minimal relevant effect size δ\delta in mind. As long as the e-variables themselves are chosen according to a GRO criterion, such a use of power as a ‘secondary’ criterion used merely to determine sample size is consistent with the GRO approach. In order for e-variables to be embraced by practitioners, we would hope that the sample sizes required to achieve a certain desired power with GRO-e-variables would be competitive with the standard approach based on Neyman-Pearson tests. We now study whether this is the case. For simplicity we only consider the Gaussian location model of Example 3, where ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is the standard normal N⁡(0,1)N(0,1) and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} the set {pμ:μ∈Θ}\{p_{\mu}:\mu\in\Theta\} of normals with variance 11. All results readily generalise to 1-dimensional exponential families.

Power: planning for a Fixed nn

For comparison, recall that a standard one-sided NP test at level α\alpha would reject if μ^≥zα/n\hat{\mu}\geq z_{\alpha}/\sqrt{n} with zαz_{\alpha} the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of the standard normal with z0.05=1.645,z0.01=2.33z_{0.05}=1.645,z_{0.01}=2.33. By standard calculation (see Appendix B.4), under an alternative with mean ≥δ\geq\delta, the sample size needed with this test to get power at least 1−β1-\beta satisfies nnp=Cnp/δ2n_{\text{\it np}}=C_{\text{\it np}}/\delta^{2} with Cnp=(zα+zβ)2C_{\text{\it np}}=(z_{\alpha}+z_{\beta})^{2}; for α=0.05,β=0.2\alpha=0.05,\beta=0.2 we get Cnp≈6.180C_{\text{\it np}}\approx 6.180. For the same Θ1={μ:μ≥δ}\Theta_{1}=\{\mu:\mu\geq\delta\}, we can also calculate the sample size needed to get power 1−β1-\beta using the GROW e-variable of Example 4. If we use a fixed sample size nn, we reject if log⁡pδ​(Yn)/p0​(Yn)≥−log⁡α\log p_{\delta}(Y^{n})/p_{0}(Y^{n})\geq-\log\alpha. By a simple calculation, for α>1/2\alpha>1/2, the smallest nn at which we have power at least 1−β1-\beta, is given by setting

ngrow-fixed=2⋅−log⁡αδ2⋅(1+zβzα)2=cα​nnp​ with ​cα=2⋅(−log⁡α)zα2.n_{\text{\it grow-fixed}}=2\cdot\frac{-\log\alpha}{\delta^{2}}\cdot\left(1+\frac{z_{\beta}}{z_{\alpha}}\right)^{2}=c_{\alpha}n_{\text{\it np}}\text{\ with\ }c_{\alpha}=\frac{2\cdot(-\log\alpha)}{z_{\alpha}^{2}}. (32)

We have c0.05≈2.2c_{0.05}\approx 2.2; c0.01≈1.7c_{0.01}\approx 1.7 and cαc_{\alpha} very slowly converges to 11 in the limit α↓0\alpha\downarrow 0: up to a constant factor of about two we need the same amount of data as in a classical approach, and the width of the induced confidence interval is of the same order. We can therefore choose a GROW E∗E^{*} that is qualitatively more similar to a standard NP test than a standard Bayes factor approach. Using instead a standard Bayesian prior W1W_{1} on Θ1\Theta_{1} with the W1W_{1}-GRO e-variable has the advantage of not needing to specify any δ\delta in advance, but the number of samples to get power 1−β1-\beta is larger by a logarithmic factor (Appendix B.4).

The evidential target growth and the maximal power approach are not contradictory: for any particular choice of α\alpha and β\beta, there is a choice of LL such that the planned-for sample sizes become the same function of δ\delta (but of course the LL resulting from α=0.05,β=1−0.8\alpha=0.05,\beta=1-0.8 will be just as arbitrary as these choices were in the first place).

Power with Optional Stopping — a Tragedy of the Commons?

No matter the considerable advantages of being safe under optional continuation, the factor of about 22 of extra data needed to get a desired power might scare away practitioners from adopting the e-variable approach. The situation changes completely once one adopts optional stopping. As we saw in the previous section, many testing problems allow us to use e-variables that remain safe under optional stopping — and we can use the most aggressive stopping rule that stops as soon as either En≥−log⁡αE_{n}\geq-\log\alpha (and we reject) or a pre-set maximum nmaxn_{\max} is achieved (and we reject if Enmax≥−log⁡αE_{n_{\max}}\geq-\log\alpha and otherwise accept). A simple but quite accurate approximation of the resulting stopping time τ1\tau_{1} for i.i.d. data in the GROW setting of Example 4, when setting nmaxn_{\max} to ∞\infty is given by using Wald’s equality in a manner first set out by Breiman (1961); ter Schure et al. (2021) give details. It gives for data Y1,Y2,…∼PδY_{1},Y_{2},\ldots\sim P_{\delta}, that 𝐄Pδ[τ1]≈(−logα)/D(Pδ∥P0)\mathbf{E}_{P_{\delta}}[\tau_{1}]\approx(-\log\alpha)/D(P_{\delta}\|P_{0}) with D(Pδ∥P0)D(P_{\delta}\|P_{0}) the KL divergence for a single outcome. For the Gaussian location family D(Pδ∥P0)=δ2/2D(P_{\delta}\|P_{0})=\delta^{2}/2, and we get 𝐄Pδ​[τ1]≈2​(−log⁡α)/δ2\mathbf{E}_{P_{\delta}}[\tau_{1}]\approx 2(-\log\alpha)/\delta^{2}. Comparing to (32), this gives that with nmax=∞n_{\max}=\infty (so that the power of our test is 11), the expected stopping time will be in fact already smaller than the fixed stopping time we get with the Neyman-Pearson approach at power 1−β1-\beta set to 0.80.8. In practice we will choose nmax​(β)n_{\max}(\beta) to be the smallest number so that the overall procedure has power 1−β1-\beta, resulting in a stopping time τβ=min⁡{τ1,nmax​(β)}\tau_{\beta}=\min\{\tau_{1},n_{\max}(\beta)\}. The expected stopping time is then really even smaller. Figure 4 demonstrates this for the Gaussian location family. As the figure illustrates for the case β=0.8\beta=0.8, we have nmax​(β)=Cβ,δ/δ2n_{\max}(\beta)=C_{\beta,\delta}/\delta^{2} and 𝐄⁡[τβ]=Cβ,δ′/δ2\mathbf{E}[\tau_{\beta}]=C^{\prime}_{\beta,\delta}/\delta^{2} for Cβ,δC_{\beta,\delta} and Cβ,δ′C^{\prime}_{\beta,\delta} that remain within constant bounds as δ\delta varies. We can in fact heuristically derive analytic expressions (integrals) for the limits Cβ,0C_{\beta,0} and Cβ,0′C^{\prime}_{\beta,0} for δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0 by rescaling the log-likelihood process (log⁡pδ​(Xn)/p0​(Xn))n(\log p_{\delta}(X^{n})/p_{0}(X^{n}))_{n} to become compatible with a Brownian motion with drift, see Appendix B.4. These give, for β=0.2\beta=0.2, Cβ,0=8.5936C_{\beta,0}=8.5936 and Cβ,0′=4.971C^{\prime}_{\beta,0}=4.971 in accordance with Figure 4. Experiments with a logrank test (ter Schure et al., 2021), tt-test (in the vignette of RR package (Ly et al., 2020)) and 2×22\times 2 tables (Turner et al., 2021) all confirm the picture that arises from Figure 4: with e-variables based on optional stopping one needs on average less data to achieve a certain desired power, but one needs to prepare for more data in the worst-case. Taking stock, we can conclude that if current standard null hypothesis tests were replaced by e-value-based tests, and the standard practice to determine study sizes were replaced by the one above, and the percentage of studies in which the alternative is true is not too small, the world would need on average about the same or even a bit less data than it does now, to reach substantially more robust conclusions and better meta-analyses. Yet — at least as long as scientists insist on power and significance requirements — each individual study would have to plan for substantially more data, giving researchers an incentive not to adapt these new methods. We see this Tragedy of the Commons as one of the biggest obstacles for uptake of e-variables in practical settings.

7 Earlier and Related Work

e-Variables, Test Martingales, Information Projections, General Novelty

As seen in Section 1.3, e-variables are the building blocks of test (super-) martingales, which go back to Ville (1939). E-variables themselves have probably been originally introduced by Levin (of PP vs N​PNP fame) (1976) (see also (Gács, 2005)) under the name test of randomness, but Levin’s abstract context is quite different from ours. Independently discovered by Zhang et al. (2011) (under the name PBR (prediction-based ratio)) they were later analyzed by Shafer et al. (2011) (calling them, with hindsight confusingly, Bayes factors); Shafer and Vovk (2019), Vovk and Wang (2021) (e-variables/values) and Shafer (2021) (bets/betting scores) — we originally called them SS-values ourselves. The literature seems to converge to e-variables and -values. Here the e may either stand for evidence or for expectation.

Test martingales themselves have been thoroughly investigated by Shafer et al. (2011), Shafer and Vovk (2019). They themselves underlie AV (anytime-valid) p-values (Johari et al., 2021), AV tests (which we call ‘tests that are safe for optional stopping’) and AV confidence sequences. The latter were recently developed in great generality by A. Ramdas and collaborators; see e.g. (Balsubramani and Ramdas, 2016, Howard et al., 2021). Both AV tests and confidence sequences have first been developed by H. Robbins and his students (Darling and Robbins, 1967, Lai, 1976, Robbins, 1970). Like we do for e-variables, Ramdas et al. (and also e.g. Pace and Salvan (2019)) stress the promise of AV notions for a safer kind of statistics that is significantly more robust than standard tests and confidence intervals.

Just like regular tests can be turned into confidence intervals by varying the null and ‘inverting’ the resulting tests, AV confidence sequences can be created by starting with a collection of test martingales, one for each null, and then varying the null (it is sometimes claimed that problematic aspects of null hypothesis testing are mostly due to the very idea of a ‘null hypothesis’ or a significance level (Cumming, 2012, McShane et al., 2019). Without wanting to take sides in this issue, we note that standard confidence intervals are just as unsafe under optional continuation as standard Neyman-Pearson hypothesis tests). The work on AV tests and confidence sequences is therefore very similar in spirit to ours, with our work stressing analysis at the level of batches of data rather than individual data points, and with the AV work bringing out the difference to Bayesian approaches more explicitly (AV 1−α1-\alpha-confidence intervals are typically wider than Bayesian 1−α1-\alpha-credible sets). In fact we do not claim any real novelty for the ‘safe’ or ‘AV’ setting per se: the real novelty of this paper is in the four versions of Theorem 1. As far as we know, these results are new, with the exception of a special case of the simplest version of Theorem 1 (Section 2): the case of discrete outcome spaces, simple ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and convex ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} was already formulated and proved by Zhang et al. (2011). Theorem 1 heavily builds on properties of standard- and reverse and joint information projections about which there is a rich literature, key references being Csiszár (1975), Topsøe (1979), Csiszár and Tusnády (1984), Csiszár and Matus (2003). Both the standard and the reverse information projection are special cases of FF-divergence projections, investigated in great detail in both the information-theoretic community (Rüschendorf, 1984) and the mathematical finance community (Gundel, 2005, Föllmer and Gundel, 2006); the robust optimization problems in the latter two papers, when instantiated to logarithmic utility, bear some resemblance to our GROW criterion. While the details and the motivation are quite different, it would be of interest to study the connections further.

Relation to Sequential Testing

Sequential testing (Lai, 2009, Siegmund, 2013), pioneered by Wald (1947) and Barnard, is mathematically very similar to, but conceptually quite different from, testing based on test martingales and (therefore) e-variables. Sequential tests are made for streams of data Yi,Y2,…Y_{i},Y_{2},\ldots as in Example 1 and Section 5 and are based on random processes (Si)i∈ℕ(S_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}} such that, for each ii, SiS_{i} is a conditional e-variable given Y1,…,Yi−1Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{i-1} under ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, and 1/Si1/S_{i} is a conditional e-variable given Y1,…,Yi−1Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{i-1} under ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. Of course, this two-sided e-variable property only holds in quite special cases — roughly under the same conditions as Proposition 3 (monotone likelihood ratio), i.e. in our Example 4 and for the tt-test with point prior on δ+,δ−\delta^{+},\delta^{-}. In such a setting, the sequential test based on S1,S2,…S_{1},S_{2},\ldots with prespecified parameters α,β\alpha,\beta proceeds by calculating S1,S2,…S_{1},S_{2},\ldots and stopping at τ∗\tau^{*}, the smallest τ\tau at which either Sτ≥(1−β)/αS_{\tau}\geq(1-\beta)/\alpha (‘accept’) or Sτ≤(1−α)/βS_{\tau}\leq(1-\alpha)/\beta (‘reject’). Wald showed that this test has Type I error probability bounded by α\alpha and Type II error bounded by β\beta. The reason one can stop at a smaller threshold ((1−β)/α(1-\beta)/\alpha rather than 1/α1/\alpha) is that one has to stop at τ∗\tau^{*}, Thus, the method does not allow for optional stopping in our sense: conceptually, sequential tests were designed for special, pre-specified stopping times. Still, much work in sequential testing can be re-cycled to obtain test martingales and e-values — but not always vice versa since e-variables are often not ‘two-sided’.

Related Work on Relating p-values and e-variables

Shafer et al. (2011) and Shafer and Vovk (2019) give a general formula for calibrators ff (see also Vovk and Wang (2021) and Vovk (1993), Sellke et al. (2001) for early work in this direction). These are decreasing functions f:[0,1]→[0,∞]f:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty] so that for any p-value p, E≔f⁡(p)E\coloneqq f(\text{\it p}) is an e-variable. The choice of any such calibrator is essentially arbitrary, but, following Shafer (2021), let us consider one that is especially simple: f⁡(p)=1/p−1f(p)=1/\sqrt{p}-1. For example, for any calibrator ff suggested for practice, rejection under the e-variable based test with significance level α=0.05\alpha=0.05, so that E≥20E\geq 20, would then correspond to reject only if p≤f−1​(20)=1/441=0.0023\text{\it p}\leq f^{-1}(20)=1/441=0.0023, requiring a substantial amount of additional data for rejection under a given alternative. Note that the e-variables we developed for given models in previous sections are more sensitive than such generic calibrators though. For example, consider the normal location family of the previous section. With the calibrator above, we would reject if μ^≥z0.0023/n≈2.8/n\hat{\mu}\geq z_{0.0023}/\sqrt{n}\approx 2.8/\sqrt{n}. The amount of data to plan for to obtain power 80%80\% would then be ≈(2.8/1.65)2​nnp≈3.0​nnp\approx(2.8/1.65)^{2}n_{\text{\it np}}\approx 3.0n_{\text{\it np}}, whereas for the e-value based on the normal likelihood ratio we would need ≈2.2​nnp\approx 2.2n_{\text{\it np}}, and even significantly less under optional stopping.

8 GRO: Discussion and Open Problems

In this paper we provided several motivations for our various GRO criteria as we introduced them, in Section 2–4. Here we reflect on the strength of our arguments in sequence-of-studies settings when taking the running products of the per-study GRO e-variables. Let us first consider a simple alternative QQ as in Section 2.1, so that GROW and REGROW criteria coincide with GRO. In an optional continuation (OC) context, the justification of GRO is strongest if all study outcomes 𝐘(1),𝐘(2),…{\bf Y}_{(1)},{\bf Y}_{(2)},\ldots are independent and the variances of log⁡E(m)\log E_{(m)} under QQ for the GRO e-variables E(m)E_{(m)} are not too large. As pointed out by a referee, if these variances are large, there could be prolonged periods of ‘draw-downs’ — in the gambling interpretation, independence ensures, by the law of large numbers, that asymptotically the GRO e-variables maximize our capital; but if there is high variance, there may be several studies in a row during which the product of all e-values so far remains low, a fact well-known among economists. Moreover, i.i.d. data and the seqdec property are required for another central justification of GRO in the optional stopping setting, namely Breiman’s insight that the expected stopping time before one can reject is minimized by maximizing expectation of the log capital (ter Schure et al. (2021) explain this in detail). This issue may perhaps in some cases be resolved by instead of adopting the ‘global’ GRO e-variable (among all e-variables for the null), taking an alternative e-variable that is GRO among a subset of e-variables with sufficiently low variance under QQ. Such low variance e-variables would presumably look quite different from likelihood ratios and Bayes factors though, since for given Θ0\Theta_{0}, the only e-variable that can be obtained by projecting on 𝒲⁡(Θ0)\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}) is the unconstrained GRO e-variable: e-variables that are optimal in a non-GRO sense cannot be obtained by projection, even if KL is replaced by another distance or divergence D′D^{\prime}: Corollary 2 implies that, with W0∗=arg⁡minOPENW)∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)​D′​(Q,PW)W^{*}_{0}=\arg\min_{W)\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D^{\prime}(Q;P_{W}), we have that E′=q⁡(𝐘)/pW0∗​(𝐘)E^{\prime}=q(\mathbf{Y})/p_{W^{*}_{0}}(\mathbf{Y}) does not give an E-variable unless W0∗W^{*}_{0} also minimizes the KL divergence, i.e. if E′E^{\prime} is an E-variable at all, it must be GRO.

In case ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is composite, then even if the 𝐘(j){\bf Y}_{(j)} are independent and the variances are low, there may be alternatives to GROW and REGROW that are sometimes preferable. For example, if we are in an OS setting and we use our tests as the basis for always-valid confidence intervals (see the previous section), we may want to aim for the conditional e-variables that lead to the confidence intervals that shrink to 00 at the fastest possible rate, which for regular 1-dimensional parameters of interest is usually O⁡((log⁡log⁡n)/n)O((\log\log n)/n) (Howard et al., 2021). These are not obtained by REGROW e-variables (which, by extending the reasoning of Example 5, in parametric problems achieve a width of O⁡((log⁡n)/n)O((\log n)/n)). The narrower O⁡((log⁡log⁡n)/n)O((\log\log n)/n) can be achieved by the switching strategies of Erven et al. (2012) or the stitching method used to design test martingales by Howard et al. (2021). A more precise understanding of whether such methods can also be re-understood as optimizing a variation of GRO, and more generally what meta-GRO criteria are reasonable at all, and in what situations, is needed. This includes the question of when any variation of GRO automatically provides seqdec, or close-to-seqdec specifications, allowing us to engage in OS (Example  9). Answering these questions is a major avenue for future research: it ultimately determines how widely applicable GRO criteria really are.

9 Could Fisher, Jeffreys and Neyman Have Agreed on a Curren- cy for Testing?

The three main approaches towards null hypothesis testing are Jeffreys’ Bayes factors, Fisher’s p-value-based testing and the Neyman-Pearson method. In the paper Could Fisher, Jeffreys and Neyman Have Agreed on Testing?, Berger (2003) noted that, while these methodologies seem superficially highly contradictory, there exist methods that have a place within all three. The developments in this paper lead to the conclusion that e-variable based testing — although it differs in some technical respects from Berger’s proposals — is very much in the same spirit:

Concerning the Neyman-Pearson approach: e-variables lead to tests with Type-I error guarantees at any fixed significance level α\alpha, which is also the first requirement of a Neyman-Pearson test — requiring safety under optional continuation or optional stopping simply enforces the requirement to hold over a non-pre-specified sequence of studies, which is a natural requirement in scientific applications. Since there is then no single study any more, the concept of ‘power’ looses its centrality (and may be upgraded to requiring power one), and growth-rate optimality is a natural quantitative refinement. The fact that a high growth-rate corresponds to a high value of 𝐄P1​[log⁡E]\mathbf{E}_{P_{1}}[\log E] under ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} whereas a high power corresponds to a high probability that P1​(log⁡E≥−log⁡α)P_{1}(\log E\geq-\log\alpha) also shows that GRO and power remain intimately connected in e-variable theory as well.

Concerning the Fisherian approach: here, p-values are interpreted as indicating amounts of evidence against the null, and their definition does not need to refer to any specific alternative ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. Exactly the same holds for e-values: the basic interpretation ‘a large e-value provides evidence against ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}’ holds no matter how the e-variable is defined, as long as it satisfies (1). If they are defined relative to ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} that is close to the actual process generating the data they will grow fast and provide a lot of evidence, but the basic interpretation holds regardless. In contrast to evidence based on standard p-values however, (a) e-based evidence has a concrete additional interpretation in terms of money (the higher EE, the more money one has gained in a game that is not favourable under the null); (b) it remains valid under optional continuation, and (c) unlike the p-value, it is compatible with (provides the same evidence as) likelihood ratios do in simple-vs.-simple testing — the one case where the use of likelihood ratio as evidence is standard.

Concerning the Bayesian approach: despite their monetary interpretation, all e-variables that we encountered can also be written as Bayes factors, and Theorem 1 strongly suggests that this is a very general phenomenon. Subjective prior knowledge can be accounted for using the W1W_{1}-GRO e-variable (Section 2.2), whereas maximin optimal GROW and REGROW e-variables sometimes correspond to ‘objective’ Bayes approaches based on Jeffreys’ and/or right-Haar priors. Still, there seem to be two fundamental differences: first, in a standard Bayesian analysis, one would require error guarantees and safety under OC under the prior instead of under all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, and second, one would insist on using full, standard likelihoods — whereas e-variables may also be based on partial (ter Schure et al., 2021) or Dawid’s (1997) prequential (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2021) likelihoods rather than full likelihoods — which then however may be combined with priors (on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}) after all. Even though we emphasise Type-I error safety throughout, because of this generic freedom in using priors on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} the link to Bayesian methods remains close.

The Dream

With the massive criticisms of p-values in recent years, there seems to be growing consensus that, in the context of hypothesis testing, p-values should either not be used at all, or at least, with utter care (Wasserstein et al., 2016, Benjamin et al., 2018). Yet otherwise, the disputes among adherents of the three schools continue. For example, some highly accomplished statisticians reject the idea of testing without a clear alternative outright; others say that such goodness-of-fit tests are an essential part of data analysis. Some insist that significance testing (with binary decisions) should be abolished altogether (Amrhein et al., 2019), others (perhaps slightly cynically) acknowledge that significance may be silly in principle, yet maintain that journals and conferences will always require a significance-style ‘bar’ in practice and that therefore such bars should be made as meaningful as possible. Finally, within the Bayesian community, the Bayes factor is sometimes presented as a panacea for most testing ills, while others warn against its use, protesting, for example, against claims that Bayes factors can ‘handle optional stopping’ (Hendriksen et al., 2021). Wouldn’t it be nice if all these accomplished but disagreeing people could continue to go their way, yet would have a common language or ‘currency’ to express amounts of evidence, and would be able to combine their results in a meaningful way? This is what e-variables can provide: consider three tests with the same null hypothesis ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}, based on samples 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)}, 𝐘(2)\mathbf{Y}_{(2)} and 𝐘(3)\mathbf{Y}_{(3)} respectively. The results of a GROW e-variable test aimed to optimise power on sample 𝐘(1)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)} for δ≥δ+\delta\geq\delta^{+}, an e-variable test for sample 𝐘(2)\mathbf{Y}_{(2)} based on a Bayesian prior W1W_{1} on ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and a Fisherian e-variable test in which the alternative ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} is not explicitly formulated, can all be multiplied — and the result will be meaningful, both in terms of monetary gain and in terms of error probability.

Appendix

Appendix A Theorem 1, Corollaries and Conditions

Here we prove Theorem 1 and its Corollary 2. We also, in Appendix A.3, discuss the required regularity conditions for Theorem 1 and we prove that they are applicable in all our examples.

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1, Simplest Version, and Corollary 2

The proof of the first version of Theorem 1 relies on quite technical results from Li (1999), but if the minimum in (11) is achieved by some prior W0∗W^{*}_{0}, and under the further condition that we can exchange differentiation and expectation, then the partial and crucial result that (10) is an e-variable has a very simple proof, which we provide first as a ‘warm-up’: evaluate the derivative f(α)=(d/α)D(Q∥(1−α)PW0∗+αPθ)f(\alpha)=(d/\alpha)D(Q\|(1-\alpha)P_{W^{*}_{0}}+\alpha P_{\theta}) at α=0\alpha=0 for arbitrary θ∈Θ0\theta\in\Theta_{0} and note that it is ≥0\geq 0 iff 𝐄𝐘∼𝐐​[pθ​(𝐘)/pW0∗​(𝐘)]=𝐄𝐘∼𝐏θ​[q⁡(𝐘)/pW0∗​(𝐘)]≤1\mathbf{E}_{\bf Y\sim Q}[p_{\theta}({\bf Y})/p_{W^{*}_{0}}({\bf Y})]=\mathbf{E}_{\bf Y\sim P_{\theta}}[q({\bf Y})/p_{W^{*}_{0}}({\bf Y})]\leq 1. Differentiating again gives that f⁡(α)f(\alpha) is convex, and the result follows from convexity of 𝒫0:={PW:W∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)}\mathcal{P}_{0}:=\{P_{W}:W\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})\}.

We proceed to give the complete and fully general proof. Note that 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} is convex, and (by assumption of the theorem) every distribution in 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} as well as QQ has a density relative to μ\mu and infP∈𝒫0D(Q∥P)<∞\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{0}}D(Q\|P)<\infty. These three givens allow us to use a range of results about the reverse information projection (RIPr) established in the Ph.D. thesis (Li, 1999) (additional proofs of (extensions of) all of Li’s results we need below can be found in the refereed paper Grünwald and Mehta (2020)).

First, the existence and uniqueness of a measure P0∗P^{*}_{0} (not necessarily a probability measure) with density p0∗p^{*}_{0} that satisfies D(Q∥P0∗)=infP∈𝒫0D(Q∥P)D(Q\|P^{*}_{0})=\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{0}}D(Q\|P) (i.e. it is the RIPr), and furthermore has the property

for all p that are densities of some P∈𝒫0:𝐄𝐘∼Q[p⁡(𝐘)p0∗​(𝐘)]≤1,\text{for all $p$ that are densities of some $P\in\mathcal{P}_{0}$:}\ \ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim Q}\left[\frac{p(\mathbf{Y})}{p^{*}_{0}(\mathbf{Y})}\right]\leq 1, (33)

follows directly from (Li, 1999, Theorem 4.3). But by writing out the integral in the expectation explicitly we immediately see that we can rewrite (33) as:

for all P∈𝒫0:𝐄𝐘∼P[q⁡(𝐘)p0∗​(𝐘)]≤1.\text{for all $P\in\mathcal{P}_{0}$:}\ \ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P}\left[\frac{q(\mathbf{Y})}{p^{*}_{0}(\mathbf{Y})}\right]\leq 1.

Li’s Theorem 4.3 still allows for the possibility that ∫p0∗​(y)​d​μ​(y)>1\int p^{*}_{0}(y)\,\textnormal{d}\mu(y)>1. To see that in fact this is impossible, i.e. p0∗p^{*}_{0} defines a (sub-) probability density, use Lemma 4.5 of Li (1999). This shows that E∗=q⁡(𝐘)/p0∗​(𝐘)E^{*}=q(\mathbf{Y})/p^{*}_{0}(\mathbf{Y}) is an e-variable, and (using that P0∗P^{*}_{0} is the RIPr) the second and third equality of (11). The final line of the result (‘if …\ldots then P0∗=PW0∗P^{*}_{0}=P_{W^{*}_{0}}’) follows directly from Lemma 4.1 of Li (1999).

It remains to show the first equality of (11) and essential uniqueness of E∗E^{*}. For the former, it is sufficient to show that for all e-variables, i.e. all E∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0}),

𝐄𝐘∼Q​[log⁡E]≤𝐄Q​[log⁡E∗].\displaystyle\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim Q}\left[\log E\right]\leq\mathbf{E}_{Q}\left[\log E^{*}\right]. (34)

To show this, fix any e-variable E=e⁡(𝐘)E=e(\mathbf{Y}) in ℰ⁡(Θ0)\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0}). Now further fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and fix a W(ϵ)∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)W_{(\epsilon)}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}) with D(Q∥PW(ϵ))≤infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)+ϵD(Q\|P_{W_{(\epsilon)}})\leq\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})+\epsilon. We must have, with q′​(y)≔e⁡(y)​pW(ϵ)​(y)q^{\prime}(y)\coloneqq e(y)p_{W_{(\epsilon)}}(y), that ∫q′​(y)​d​μ=𝐄𝐘∼PW(ϵ)​[E]≤1\int q^{\prime}(y)\,\textnormal{d}\mu=\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W_{(\epsilon)}}}[E]\leq 1, so q′q^{\prime} is a sub-probability density, and by properness of the log scoring rule,

𝐄Q[logE]=𝐄Q[logq′​(𝐘)pW(ϵ)​(𝐘)]≤𝐄Q[logq⁡(𝐘)pW(ϵ)​(𝐘)]=D(Q∥PW(ϵ))≤infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(Q∥PW0)+ϵ.\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E]=\mathbf{E}_{Q}\left[\log\frac{q^{\prime}(\mathbf{Y})}{p_{W_{(\epsilon)}}(\mathbf{Y})}\right]\leq\\ \mathbf{E}_{Q}\left[\log\frac{q(\mathbf{Y})}{p_{W_{(\epsilon)}}(\mathbf{Y})}\right]=D(Q\|P_{W_{(\epsilon)}})\leq\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})+\epsilon.

Since we can take ϵ\epsilon to be arbitrarily close to 00, (34) follows.

To show essential uniqueness of E∗E^{*}, let EE be any e-variable with 𝐄Q​[log⁡E]=𝐄Q​[log⁡E∗]\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E]=\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E^{*}]. By linearity of expectation, E′=(1/2)​E∗+(1/2)​EE^{\prime}=(1/2)E^{*}+(1/2)E is then also an e-variable, and by Jensen’s inequality applied to the logarithm we must have 𝐄Q​[log⁡E′]>𝐄Q​[log⁡E∗]\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E^{\prime}]>\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E^{*}] unless Q⁡(E=E∗)=1Q(E=E^{*})=1. Since we have already shown that for any e-variable E′E^{\prime}, 𝐄Q​[log⁡E′]≤𝐄Q​[log⁡E∗]\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E^{\prime}]\leq\mathbf{E}_{Q}[\log E^{*}], it follows that Q⁡(E≠E∗)=0Q(E\neq E^{*})=0. But then, by our assumption that QQ has full support, i.e. q⁡(𝐘)>0q({\bf Y})>0 hold μ\mu-almost everywhere, we must have that Pθ​(E≠E∗)=0P_{\theta}(E\neq E^{*})=0 for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, so E∗E^{*} is essentially unique.

Proof of Corollary 2

Let W0W_{0} be as in the corollary statement. By definition of E∗E^{*} as in Theorem 1, simplest version, and then using strict convexity of the KL divergence in its second argument (Cover and Thomas, 1991) and the fact that D(Q∥P)D(Q\|P) is minimised, over P∈{PW:W∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)}P\in\{P_{W}:W\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})\}, we have:

𝐄Q[logE∗]=D(Q∥P0∗)<D(Q∥PW0)=𝐄Q[logqpW0]\mathbf{E}_{Q}\left[\log E^{*}\right]=D(Q\|P^{*}_{0})<D(Q\|P_{W_{0}})=\mathbf{E}_{Q}\left[\log\frac{q}{p_{W_{0}}}\right]

so that, if q/pW0{q}/{p_{W_{0}}} were an e-variable, we would have a contradiction with the first equality in (11).

A.2 Proof of full version of Theorem 1

The proof consists of two sub-parts, Part (a) relying on the simple version of the theorem presented in Section 2 and proven above (henceforth called ‘the simple theorem’), and Part (b) relying on a nonstandard minimax/saddle-point theorem from Grünwald and Dawid (2004) (GD from now on), itself relying heavily on an earlier result from Topsøe (1979).

Part (a). We first show that EfE^{f} as in (26) is an e-variable. This follows by the simple theorem, with 𝐕\mathbf{V} in the role of 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, QQ in the theorem statement substituted by PW1∗[𝐕]P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W_{1}^{*}} and PWP_{W} for W∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)W\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}) replaced by PW[𝐕]P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W} and using that (25) implies that infW0∈𝒲0​(Θ0)D(PW1∗[𝐕]∥PW0[𝐕])<∞\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}_{0}(\Theta_{0})}D(P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W_{0}})<\infty. Next, we show that if (27) holds for EfE^{f} as in (26), then all e-variables EE for which it holds must be essentially equal to EfE^{f}. To see this, suppose that EE is another e-variable satisfying (27). Then we have

infW∈𝒲1(𝐄𝐘∼PW[logE]−f(W))=D(PW1∗[𝐕]∥P0∗[𝐕])−f(W1∗)=𝐄𝐘∼PW1∗[logEf]−f(W1∗)\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W}}[\log E]-f(W)\ )=D(P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{*[\mathbf{V}]}_{0})-f(W^{*}_{1})=\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W^{*}_{1}}}\left[\log E^{f}\right]-f(W^{*}_{1})

as follows by writing out the definition of D(⋅∥⋅)D(\cdot\|\cdot). On the other hand, using the definition of inf\inf, we must have

infW∈𝒲1(𝐄𝐘∼PW​[log⁡E]−f⁡(W))≤𝐄𝐘∼PW1∗​[log⁡E]−f⁡(W1∗).\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W}}[\log E]-f(W)\ )\leq\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W^{*}_{1}}}\left[\log E\right]-f(W^{*}_{1}).

The only way these two displays can be reconciled is if 𝐄𝐘∼PW1∗​[log⁡E]≥𝐄𝐘∼PW1∗​[log⁡Ef]\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W^{*}_{1}}}\left[\log E\right]\geq\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W^{*}_{1}}}\left[\log E^{f}\right]. But since EfE^{f} is the RIPr of PW1∗[𝐕]P_{W_{1}^{*}}^{[\mathbf{V}]}, we can use the simple theorem again, applied with PW1∗P_{W_{1}^{*}} in the role of QQ and ℋ1={PW1∗}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{W_{1}^{*}}\}, to conclude that EfE^{f} must be essentially equal to EE. The final line of the fully general Theorem 1 follows again by reduction to the analogous statement of the simple theorem.

Finally, we will use the simple theorem to show the following one-sided version of (27):

infW∈𝒲1(𝐄𝐘∼PW[logEf]−f(W))≤supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)infW∈𝒲1(𝐄𝐘∼PW[logE]−f(W))≤D(PW1∗[𝐕]∥P0∗[𝐕])−f(W1∗).\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W}}[\log E^{f}]-f(W)\ )\leq\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}(\ \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{Y}\sim P_{W}}[\log E]-f(W)\ )\leq\\ D(P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{*[\mathbf{V}]}_{0})-f(W^{*}_{1}). (35)

The first inequality is trivial since Ef∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)E^{f}\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0}). The second follows if we can show that

supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)infW∈𝒲1𝐄PW[logE−f(W)]≤infW∈𝒲1infW0∈𝒲0(D(PW∥PW0)−f(W1))\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{P_{W}}[\log E-f(W)]\leq\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}_{0}}(\ D(P_{W}\|P_{W_{0}})-f(W_{1})\ ) (36)

and recognizing that by assumptions of the theorem, the right-hand side of (36) coincides with the right-hand side of (35). To prove (36), note that by the simple version of the theorem we already have for each fixed W1∈𝒲1W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}_{1} that

infW0∈𝒲0D(PW1∥PW0)=supE∈ℰ⁡(Θ0)𝐄PW1[logE]\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}_{0}}D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})=\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}(\Theta_{0})}\mathbf{E}_{P_{W_{1}}}[\log E]

and this directly implies the inequality by adding −f⁡(W1)-f(W_{1}) to both sides and using a standard “infsup≥supinf\inf\sup\geq\sup\inf” argument (the trivial side of the minimax theorem). The equality follows by assumption of the Theorem.

Part (b). Taking stock, we see that the only thing that is left to prove is (35) with the reversed inequalities. For this, it suffices to show that

D(PW1∗[𝐕]∥P0∗[𝐕])−f(W1∗)≤infW∈𝒲1𝐄PW[logEf−f(W)].D(P^{[\mathbf{V}]}_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P^{*[\mathbf{V}]}_{0})-f(W^{*}_{1})\leq\inf_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}\mathbf{E}_{P_{W}}[\log E^{f}-f(W)]. (37)

Since all distributions occurring in (37) are marginals on 𝐕\mathbf{V}, and EfE^{f} can be written as a function of 𝐕\mathbf{V}, we will from now on simply refer to the marginal densities on 𝐕\mathbf{V} corresponding to PWP_{W} as pWp_{W} (rather than pW′p^{\prime}_{W} as in the main text), and we will omit the superscripts [𝐕][\mathbf{V}] from PP; thus we take as our basic outcome now 𝐕\mathbf{V} rather than 𝐘\mathbf{Y}.

We will show the stronger statement that (37) holds with equality, by using a minimax/saddle point result that holds for general functions L:Θ1×𝒲1→ℝ∪{∞}L:\Theta_{1}\times\mathcal{W}_{1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\{\infty\} such that L⁡(Wn,Wu):=𝐄θ∼Wn​[L⁡(θ,Wu)]L(W_{\text{\sc n}},W_{\text{\sc u}}):=\mathbf{E}_{\theta\sim W_{\text{\sc n}}}[L(\theta,W_{\text{\sc u}})] is well-defined for all Wn∈𝒲1W_{\text{\sc n}}\in\mathcal{W}_{1} (the condition ‘well-defined’ is necessary since the expectation is over a function that may neither be bounded from below nor from above; see for example Section 3.1 of GD for the (standard) definitions). These LL are interpreted as loss functions, with θ1∈Θ1\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1} denoting a state of nature and 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1} an arbitrary convex set of distributions on Θ1\Theta_{1}, each W∈𝒲1W\in\mathcal{W}_{1} being interpreted as an action. Following GD, we can associate a decision-theoretic entropy H⁡(Wn):=infWu∈𝒲L0​(Wn,Wu)=L⁡(Wn,Wn)H(W_{\text{\sc n}}):=\inf_{W_{\text{\sc u}}\in\mathcal{W}}L_{0}(W_{\text{\sc n}},W_{\text{\sc u}})=L(W_{\text{\sc n}},W_{\text{\sc n}}) with any such LL. The following result holds for all Θ1\Theta_{1}, 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1} and LL as defined above but we will apply it to the instantiation of Θ1\Theta_{1} and 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1} in Theorem 1.

GD’s Theorem 6.3

Assume that (a) LL is a proper scoring rule, i.e. for all Wn∈𝒲1W_{\text{\sc n}}\in\mathcal{W}_{1}, H⁡(Wn)=L⁡(Wn,Wn)H(W_{\text{\sc n}})=L(W_{\text{\sc n}},W_{\text{\sc n}}). Suppose that (b) W1∗∈𝒲1W_{1}^{*}\in\mathcal{W}_{1} is ‘maximum entropy’ i.e. supWn∈𝒲1H⁡(Wn)=H⁡(W1∗)<∞\sup_{W_{\text{\sc n}}\in\mathcal{W}_{1}}H(W_{\text{\sc n}})=H(W^{*}_{1})<\infty and (c) the lower semi-continuity condition below holds. Then (W1∗,W1∗)(W_{1}^{*},W_{1}^{*}) is a saddle-point relative to LL, i.e.

(25) implies that D(PW1∗∥P0∗)<∞D(P_{W_{1}^{*}}\|P^{*}_{0})<\infty for some P0∗P^{*}_{0} with density p0∗p^{*}_{0}. Similarly, PWP_{W} must have some density pWp_{W} under all W∈𝒲1W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}. Applying GD’s theorem to LL

We apply GD’s theorem to the loss function LL above with W1∗W_{1}^{*} as in the statement of the theorem. From (39) we see that L⁡(W1∗,W)L(W^{*}_{1},W) is minimised, over 𝒲1\mathcal{W}_{1}, by W=W1∗W=W^{*}_{1} and then finite, so that GD’s requirements (a) and (b) hold for loss function LL. which, rewriting the left-hand side using (39) and the right-hand side using definition of LL, is in turn seen to be equivalent to (37), and the desired result follows.

It thus only remains to show that the lower semicontinuity condition holds.
