Next, using (39), we see that it is sufficient to show that for all W∈𝒲1W\in\mathcal{W}_{1}:

D(PW∥PW∘)≤liminfn→∞D(PW∥PWn).D(P_{W}\|P_{W^{\circ}})\leq\lim\inf_{n\rightarrow\infty}D(P_{W}\|P_{W_{n}}).

But this again follows directly from Posner’s theorem, which also says that KL divergence is lower semi-continuous in its second argument.

A.3 Remarks on and Checking of Conditions for Theorem 1

The Full Support and Finite KL Condition

Requiring full support in the simplest version of the theorem ensures that E∗E^{*} is a.s. well-defined: without it, there may be an outcome 𝐲{\bf y} such that for some θ∈Θ0\theta\in\Theta_{0}, Pθ​(𝐲)>0P_{\theta}({\bf y})>0 whereas PW0​(𝐲)=Q⁡(𝐲)=0P_{W_{0}}({\bf y})=Q({\bf y})=0. Then E∗E^{*} is undefined with positive probability under this θ\theta. The finite KL condition D(Pθ∥Pθ′)<∞D(P_{\theta}\|P_{\theta^{\prime}})<\infty imposed in the generalised versions of the theorem is just slightly stronger than the full support condition. It is required to make sure that all expectations in the proof are well-defined.

For standard parametric models in standard parameterisations (e.g. all multivariate exponential families in their mean-value parameterisation), both conditions will hold automatically as long as one excludes points at the boundary of the parameter space, if those exist. For example, in the 2×22\times 2 setting without a pre-specified effect size we restrict Θ1\Theta_{1} to (0,1)2(0,1)^{2}, requiring the Bernoulli probabilities μ1|a\mu_{1|a} and μ1|b\mu_{1|b} to be non-degenerate. But, since the condition only refers to Θ1\Theta_{1}, it is o.k. to set Θ0=[0,1]\Theta_{0}=[0,1] to include the boundary points in the null.

Additional Condition: Existence of W1∗W^{*}_{1}

The requirement for composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} that a W1∗{W^{*}_{1}} exists achieving the minimum in (27) is strong in general, but it holds in all our examples with composite ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}: Example 4 (W1∗W_{1}^{*} is shown to be a point prior in the example), Example 5 (since there we restrict Θ1\Theta_{1} to be compact) and Example 6 and 7 (here verifying the condition requires some work, see below). It also holds in the tt-test setting underneath Theorem 2 with effect sizes δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-} (W1∗W_{1}^{*} reduces to a point prior on δ+\delta^{+}). By allowing e-variables to be functions of 𝐕\mathbf{V} that are themselves functions of 𝐘\mathbf{Y} (i.e. σ⁡(𝐘)\sigma(\mathbf{Y})-measurable) as in the latter example, we make the condition considerably weaker.

Applicability of Theorem 1 and existence of minimizing W1∗W^{*}_{1} and W0∗W^{*}_{0} in Example 6 and 7

We have ℋ1={Pμ1|a,μ1|b:(μ1|a,μ1|b)∈Θ1}\mathcal{H}_{1}=\{P_{\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}}:(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})\in\Theta_{1}\} and ℋ0={Pμ:μ∈Θ0}\mathcal{H}_{0}=\{P_{\mu}:\mu\in\Theta_{0}\}, Θ0=[0,1]\Theta_{0}=[0,1] with definitions as in Example 2. In Example 6, we take Θ1=(0,1)2\Theta_{1}=(0,1)^{2} and we can take Θ0=[0,1]\Theta_{0}=[0,1] or Θ0=(0,1)\Theta_{0}=(0,1) (the same minima will be achieved in both cases). In Example 7 we take Θ1={(μ1|a,μ1|a+δ):0<μ1,a<1−δ}\Theta_{1}=\{(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|a}+\delta):0<\mu_{1,a}<1-\delta\} and Θ0=(0,1)\Theta_{0}=(0,1).

We only give the proof for Example 6; the proof for Example 7 is entirely analogous.

The requirement for applying Theorem 1 that Pθ,Pθ′P_{\theta},P_{\theta^{\prime}} with θ,θ′∈Θ1\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\Theta_{1} satisfy D(Pθ∥Pθ′)<∞D(P_{\theta}\|P_{\theta^{\prime}})<\infty, and have full support trivially holds by our exclusion of the boundary points in Θ1\Theta_{1}. The only remaining condition for applying Theorem 1 is the existence of a KL minimizing prior W1∗W^{*}_{1}. We will show the stronger result that there exists a pair of minimizing priors (W1∗,W0∗)(W^{*}_{1},W^{*}_{0}) with W1∗∈𝒲⁡(Θ1)W^{*}_{1}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}) and W0∗∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)W^{*}_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}) such that

infW1∈𝒲⁡(Θ1),W0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)(D(PW1∥PW0)−f(W1))=D(PW1∗∥PW0∗)−f(W1∗)<∞,\inf_{W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}),W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}(D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})-f(W_{1}))=D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W^{*}_{0}})-f(W^{*}_{1})<\infty, (40)

with f⁡(W)=𝐄(μ1|a,μ1|b)∼W​[f⁡(μ1|a,μ1|b)]f(W)=\mathbf{E}_{(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})\sim W}[f(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})] and f(μ1|a,μ1|b)=D(Pμ1|a,μ1|b∥Pμ∘)f(\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b})=D(P_{\mu_{1|a},\mu_{1|b}}\|P_{\mu^{\circ}}) with μ∘\mu^{\circ} as in (14). We do this by first, in Part (a), showing that there exists such a pair with W1∗∈[0,1]2W^{*}_{1}\in[0,1]^{2}, i.e. with Θ1\Theta_{1} extended to include its boundary points. We then, in Part (b), show that the resulting W1∗W^{*}_{1} puts no mass on these boundary points, so that it also achieves the minimum on 𝒲⁡(Θ1)\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}).

Part (a) The sets 𝒲⁡([0,1]2)\mathcal{W}([0,1]^{2}) and 𝒲⁡(Θ0)\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}) are convex and compact in the weak topology; by Posner’s (1975) theorem, D(PW1∥PW0)D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}}) is lower-semicontinuous in its second argument in the weak topology on {PW0:W0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)}\{P_{W_{0}}:W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})\} and hence on 𝒲⁡(Θ0)\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}) itself (see Section 9 of GD) and f⁡(W)f(W) is linear and bounded on 𝒲⁡(Θ0)\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0}); this shows that for each W1W_{1}, the corresponding minimizing W0∗W^{*}_{0} is achieved; since D(PW1∥PW0∗)≤D(PW1∥P1/2)<∞D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W^{*}_{0}})\leq D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{1/2})<\infty (with P1/2∈ℋ0P_{1/2}\in\mathcal{H}_{0} representing Bernoulli(1/2)(1/2)) and ff is bounded, the finiteness in (40) is guaranteed as well. To see that the minimum W1W_{1} is achieved as well, note that, again by Posner’s theorem, D(PW1∥PW0)D(P_{W_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}}) is also lower-semicontinuous in its first argument in the weak topology on {PW1:W1∈𝒲⁡([0,1]2)}\{P_{W_{1}}:W_{1}\in\mathcal{W}([0,1]^{2})\}. The same argument as before now gives that the minimum W1∗W^{*}_{1} is achieved.

Part (b) It now suffices to show that PW1∗P_{W^{*}_{1}} has full support, for this implies that W1∗W^{*}_{1} assigns mass 11 on Θ1=(0,1)2\Theta_{1}=(0,1)^{2} and then W0∗W^{*}_{0} must assign mass 11 on (0,1)(0,1) (otherwise the KL divergence in (40) would be infinite, and we already established it is not). To show full support of PW1∗P_{W^{*}_{1}}, note that by symmetry considerations, we must have that, with our choice of ff,

M:=D(PW1∗∥PW0∗)−f(W1∗)=D(PW1∘∥PW0∘)−f(W1∘)M:=D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W^{*}_{0}})-f(W^{*}_{1})=D(P_{W^{\circ}_{1}}\|P_{W^{\circ}_{0}})-f(W^{\circ}_{1}) (41)

for a prior W1∘W^{\circ}_{1} such that, for all 𝐲∈{0,1}n{\bf y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, pW1∘​(𝐲∣𝐱)=pW1∗​(𝐲′∣𝐱)p_{W^{\circ}_{1}}({\bf y}\mid{\bf x})=p_{W^{*}_{1}}({\bf y}^{\prime}\mid{\bf x}) with 𝐲′{\bf y}^{\prime} is the modification of 𝐲{\bf y} with all 00s and 11s interchanged, and similarly for W0∘W^{\circ}_{0}. Now if PW1∗P_{W^{*}_{1}} would not have full support, we have PW1∗(Y1=y1,Y2=y2∣X1=a,X2=b)=0P_{W^{*}_{1}}(Y_{1}=y_{1},Y_{2}=y_{2}\mid X_{1}=a,X_{2}=b)=0 for some (y1,y2)∈{0,1}2(y_{1},y_{2})\in\{0,1\}^{2}. Then PW1∘(Y1=y¯1,Y2=y¯2∣X1=a,X2=b)=0P_{W^{\circ}_{1}}(Y_{1}=\bar{y}_{1},Y_{2}=\bar{y}_{2}\mid X_{1}=a,X_{2}=b)=0 for y¯j=1−yj\bar{y}_{j}=1-y_{j}. But infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW1∗∥PW0)−f(W1∗)\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W^{*}_{1}}\|P_{W_{0}})-f(W^{*}_{1}) as a function of W1∗W^{*}_{1} is easily checked to be strictly convex on 𝒲⁡(Θ1)\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}), so by (41) we must have that, for W′=(1/2)​W1∗+(1/2)​W1∘W^{\prime}=(1/2)W^{*}_{1}+(1/2)W^{\circ}_{1}, it holds that infW0∈𝒲⁡(Θ0)D(PW′∥PW0)+f(W′)<M\inf_{W_{0}\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{0})}D(P_{W^{\prime}}\|P_{W_{0}})+f(W^{\prime})<M. But this contradicts that MM is the minimum. This shows that PW1∗P_{W^{*}_{1}} has full support.

Finiteness of Support in Example 6 and 7

We claimed that the supports of the priors W1∗W^{*}_{1} and W0∗W^{*}_{0} in Example 7 (restricted Θ1\Theta_{1}) are finite. In fact they are finite also in Example 6 (unrestricted Θ1\Theta_{1}). We verify this for W1∗W^{*}_{1}, the case for W0∗W^{*}_{0} is analogous. Note that for given sample size nn, the probability distribution PWP_{W} is completely determined by the probabilities assigned to the sufficient statistics N1|a,N1|bN_{1|a},N_{1|b}. This means that for each prior W∈𝒲⁡(Θ1)W\in\mathcal{W}(\Theta_{1}), the Bayes marginal PWP_{W} can be identified with a vector of Mn≔(na+1)⋅(nb+1)M_{n}\coloneqq(n_{a}+1)\cdot(n_{b}+1) real-valued components. Every such PWP_{W} can also be written as a mixture of PθP_{\theta}’s for θ=(μa|1,μb|1)∈Θ1\theta=(\mu_{a|1},\mu_{b|1})\in\Theta_{1}, a convex set. By Carathéodory’s theorem we need at most MnM_{n} mixture components to describe an arbitrary PWP_{W} as a mixture of the PθP_{\theta}’s; this proves the claim.

Appendix B Additional Clarifications and Proofs

B.1 Section 1.3

We discuss two extensions of the filtration to be used in Definition 1. For concreteness and simplicity we consider the sequential set-up of Section 5 in which, for each study mm, there is an underlying data stream Ym,1,Ym​.2,…Y_{m,1},Y_{m.2},\ldots.

Filtration: Conditional Distributions

In the 2×22\times 2 setting the Θ1\Theta_{1} represent conditional distributions of Y|XY\mid X. While neither Section 1.3 nor Section 5 formally allowed for that setting, the extension is straightforward. We simply assume the underlying streams are of the form (Xm,1,Ym,1),(Xm,2,Ym,2),…(X_{m,1},Y_{m,1}),(X_{m,2},Y_{m,2}),\ldots (with, in the 2×22\times 2 example, Xm,i∈{a,b}X_{m,i}\in\{a,b\}). The distributions in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} are now extended to define a random process of independent outcomes with the same conditional distribution for a single such stream (X1,Y1),(X2,Y2),…(X_{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2},Y_{2}),\ldots, i.e. for all θ1∈Θ1\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1}, we set pθ1​(yn∣xn)=Pθ1​(Yn=yn∣Xn=xn):=∏i=1npθ1​(yi∣xi)p_{\theta_{1}}(y^{n}\mid x^{n})=P_{\theta_{1}}(Y^{n}=y^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n}):=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_{\theta_{1}}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}). We then only need to extend Definition 1 of conditional e-variables to deal with this extension. This is achieved by setting ℱ(m−1)\mathcal{F}_{(m-1)} in the definition to σ⁡(𝐘(m−1),𝐗(m))\sigma(\mathbf{Y}^{(m-1)},\mathbf{X}^{(m)}).

Filtration: Side Information

Now we consider how the set-up can be extended to deal with side-information that may be used e.g. after jj studies to decide whether to start a new, j+1j+1st study at all, and if so, what the sample size of that study will be. For this we again need to extend ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} and ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} so that its elements define a conditional random process, with at the time that the jj-th study has just been observed, also the additional variables 𝐑(1),…,𝐑(j)\mathbf{R}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{R}_{(j)} observed. Even if there are underlying streams of data Yj,1,Yj,2,…Y_{j,1},Y_{j,2},\ldots so that the 𝐘(j)\mathbf{Y}_{(j)} have an internal structure, the 𝐑(j)\mathbf{R}_{(j)} are not required to have such a structure. To make all desired probabilities well-defined and at the same time make sure that the side-information is really external, we impose a conditional independence on the underlying stream: under each P∈ℋ0P\in\mathcal{H}_{0}, for each m,i∈ℕm,i\in\mathbb{N}, the conditional distribution of Ym,iY_{m,i} given Ymi−1Y_{m}^{i-1} and 𝐑(m−1)\mathbf{R}^{(m-1)} is defined to be the same as the distribution under PP of Ym,iY_{m,i} given Ymi−1Y_{m}^{i-1}, which is already well-defined once ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is specified. With this definition, we can set ℱ(j)=σ⁡(𝐘(j),𝐑(j))\mathcal{F}_{(j)}=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}^{(j)},\mathbf{R}^{(j)}) (or ℱ(j)=σ⁡(𝐘(j),𝐑(j),𝐗(j+1))\mathcal{F}_{(j)}=\sigma({\bf Y}^{(j)},\mathbf{R}^{(j)},\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}) if the ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} already contain conditional distributions, or ℱ(j)=σ⁡(𝐔(j),𝐑(j),𝐗(j+1))\mathcal{F}_{(j)}=\sigma({\bf U}^{(j)},\mathbf{R}^{(j)},\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}) with 𝐔(j){\bf U}^{(j)} a coarsening of 𝐘(j)\mathbf{Y}^{(j)} if required, such as in the tt-test setting). Focusing on the simplest case with ℱ(j)=σ⁡(𝐘(j),𝐑(j))\mathcal{F}_{(j)}=\sigma(\mathbf{Y}^{(j)},\mathbf{R}^{(j)}), the construction ensures that 𝐄P[E(j)∣𝐘(j−1),𝐑(j−1)]≤1\mathbf{E}_{P}[E_{(j)}\mid\mathbf{Y}^{(j-1)},\mathbf{R}^{(j-1)}]\leq 1 (and hence we have safety under OC) in both cases discussed in Section 5: we can either use the plug-in application of any e-variable specification, or, if the specification is seqdec, we can also use the sequential application. Note that with this construction, the 𝐑(j)\mathbf{R}^{(j)} are allowed to depend on 𝐘(1),…,𝐘(j)\mathbf{Y}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{Y}_{(j)} in unspecified ways. This is unproblematic because (other than in the case with conditional distributions and 𝐗(j+1)\mathbf{X}^{(j+1)}) the E(j+1)E_{(j+1)} cannot depend on 𝐑(j+1)\mathbf{R}^{(j+1)}. For example, based on what she sees in the 𝐘(j)\mathbf{Y}_{(j)}, your boss may decide to announce ‘we have money to do an additional study with 100 patients’, which can be encoded as a particular outcome of 𝐑(j)\mathbf{R}_{(j)}. This may then be used to decide to continue (i.e. set τ\tau in Proposition 2 to be larger than jj) and set N(j+1)N_{(j+1)} to be 100100.

Applicability of Proposition 3 to the tt-test Setting

(Section 4.3 underneath Theorem 2) A simple calculation gives that pδ+′​(𝐕)/pδ−′​(𝐕)p^{\prime}_{\delta^{+}}(\mathbf{V})/p^{\prime}_{\delta^{-}}(\mathbf{V}) can be re-expressed as a density ratio of the tt-statistic T=t⁡(𝐘)T=t(\bf Y), i.e. pδ+′​(𝐕)/pδ−′​(𝐕)=pδ+′′​(t⁡(𝐘))/pδ−′​(t⁡(𝐘))p^{\prime}_{\delta^{+}}(\mathbf{V})/p^{\prime}_{\delta^{-}}(\mathbf{V})=p^{\prime\prime}_{\delta^{+}}(t(\mathbf{Y}))/p^{\prime}_{\delta^{-}}(t(\mathbf{Y})), where pδ′′p^{\prime\prime}_{\delta} is the density of a noncentral tt-distribution with ν:=n−1\nu:=n-1 degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter μ=n​δ\mu=\sqrt{n}\delta. But these densities are well-known to form a monotone likelihood ratio family in the TT statistic, so that we can apply Proposition 3 to {pδ′′:δ∈Δ}\{p^{\prime\prime}_{\delta}:\delta\in\Delta\}.
